docs.title: Data Migration Tool
docs.text:
Welcome to the documentation for the M3 Data Migration Platform.

The Data Migration Tool is used to transform legacy data into formats required for migration into Infor M3.

docs.title: Main Areas
docs.text:
The application is organized into:

  • Configuration
  • Run Migration
  • Rules
  • Administration
  • Utilities
  • Troubleshooting

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: If this is your first time using the tool, start with the Getting Started section.

docs.title: Configuration Overview
docs.text:
The Configuration area defines how the Data Migration Tool connects legacy source data with the appropriate M3 migration configuration.

Configuration provides the information the application needs to determine:

  • Where the source data comes from
  • Which MCO business object is being migrated
  • Which M3 API is associated with the migration
  • Which Rule Configuration should be used
  • Which SDT template should receive the transformed data
  • Which transaction sheets are required

docs.title: Configuration in the Migration Process
docs.text:
Configuration connects the major components of a migration.

Legacy Source
      │
      ▼
Source Configuration
      │
      ▼
MCO / Business Object
      │
      ├─────────────► Rule Configuration
      │
      ▼
M3 API
      │
      ▼
SDT Template
      │
      ▼
Transaction Sheet(s)
      │
      ▼
Migration Output

Without the correct configuration, the application may not be able to determine which source, rules, API, or SDT template should be used.

docs.title: Main Configuration Components
docs.text: The Data Migration Tool uses several configuration components.

docs.title: MCO Specification
docs.text:
The MCO specification provides information about the migration business objects and their source-to-target field relationships.

The tool can analyze an MCO workbook and use that information to help create migration configurations.

docs.title: Source Map
docs.text:
The Source Map defines where the legacy data for a migration comes from.

It connects an MCO sheet or business object with its corresponding source.

The source may be:

  • Excel
  • CSV
  • SQL

Conceptually:

MCO Sheet
    │
    ▼
Source Map
    │
    ▼
Legacy Source

docs.title: Migration Map
docs.text:
The Migration Map connects the migration business object with the M3 configuration required to generate the output.

It can identify information such as:

MCO Sheet
    │
    ├──► API
    ├──► SDT Template
    └──► Transaction Sheet(s)

This allows the Migration Runner to automatically determine which SDT structure should be used.

docs.title: Rule Configuration
docs.text:
The Rule Configuration contains the transformation logic.

For example:

Legacy Source
      │
      ▼
Rule Configuration
      │
      ▼
M3 Target Values

Rule Configuration files are normally stored under:

config/rules/

See Understanding the Rule Configuration for more information.

docs.title: SDT Templates
docs.text:
SDT templates define the M3 output structure.

Templates are normally stored under:

config/sdt_templates/

The Migration Map determines which template should be associated with a migration.

docs.title: Business Units and Scope
docs.text:
Business-unit configuration allows transformation rules to vary when required.

The default rule scope is:

GLOBAL

Additional scopes can be configured for business-specific requirements.

For example:

GLOBAL
DIV_US
DIV_CA

docs.title: Database Configuration
docs.text:
The Data Migration Tool can also use SQL as a source.

Database connection information is maintained separately from the transformation rules.

A SQL source can then be used by the extraction process instead of an Excel or CSV file.

docs.title: Why Configuration Matters
docs.text:
Consider a migration for Item Master.

The tool needs to understand the complete relationship:

Item Master
    │
    ├── Where is the source data?
    │
    ├── Which M3 API applies?
    │
    ├── Which rules should be used?
    │
    ├── Which SDT template applies?
    │
    └── Which transaction sheets should be populated?

Configuration provides these relationships so they do not need to be manually specified every time a migration is executed.

docs.title: Configuration vs Rules
docs.text:
Configuration and Rules serve different purposes.

Configuration Rules Determines what migration setup to use Determines how data is transformed Identifies source Reads source values Identifies API Calculates M3 values Identifies SDT template Applies business logic Identifies transaction sheets Populates target fields

Both are required for a successful migration.

Configuration
      +
Rules
      +
Source Data
      │
      ▼
Migration Engine
      │
      ▼
M3 SDT Output

docs.title: Recommended Configuration Workflow
docs.text:
When preparing a new migration object:

  1. Review the MCO specification.
  2. Identify the legacy source.
  3. Configure the Source Map.
  4. Identify the M3 API.
  5. Configure the Migration Map.
  6. Verify the SDT template.
  7. Create or import the Rule Configuration.
  8. Review transformation rules.
  9. Test the migration.
  10. Validate the generated output.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Continue with:

  • MCO Import
  • Source Map
  • Migration Map
  • Database Configuration

docs.title: Rule Configuration Snapshots
docs.text:
A Snapshot preserves a copy of a Rule Configuration at a specific point in time.

Snapshots provide a safety mechanism when rules are being developed, modified, or tested.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Rule Configurations can contain many transformation rules.

A change to one rule may affect the generated migration output.

Before significant modifications, preserving the current configuration provides a known reference point.

Current Rules
     │
     ▼
Create Snapshot
     │
     ▼
Modify Rules
     │
     ▼
Test Changes

If necessary, the previous configuration can then be reviewed.

docs.title: When to Create a Snapshot
docs.text:
Snapshots are especially useful before:

  • Major rule changes
  • Business-unit overrides
  • Large MAP updates
  • Complex Python-rule modifications
  • Rule Configuration restructuring
  • Testing significant migration changes

For example:

Working PLCD Rule
       │
       ▼
Create Snapshot
       │
       ▼
Modify PLCD Logic
       │
       ▼
Test

docs.title: Snapshots vs Rule History
docs.text:
These concepts are related but serve different purposes.

Rule History Snapshot Tracks changes Preserves a configuration state Useful for investigation Useful as a recovery/reference point Shows evolution Represents a point in time

Together they provide better control over Rule Configuration changes.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose MMS200MI.xlsx contains validated rules.

Before implementing several new requirements:

MMS200MI.xlsx
      │
      ▼
Snapshot
      │
      ▼
Modify Rules
      │
      ├── PLCD
      ├── PUIT
      └── ORTY

If unexpected results appear, the previous snapshot provides a reference for comparing the configuration before and after the modifications.

docs.title: Snapshot Validation
docs.text:
A snapshot should not automatically be considered a valid production configuration simply because it exists.

It represents:

The Rule Configuration at a particular point in time.

The migration status at that point should still be understood.

For example:

Snapshot A
    └── Development

Snapshot B
    └── Tested

Snapshot C
    └── Production Candidate

The team should know which configuration was actually validated.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
Create meaningful snapshots around significant migration milestones.

For example:

Initial Configuration
        │
        ▼
Rules Developed
        │
        ▼
Snapshot
        │
        ▼
Business Testing
        │
        ▼
Rule Corrections
        │
        ▼
Snapshot
        │
        ▼
Final Validation

Avoid relying on memory to determine which version contained a particular transformation.

docs.title: Troubleshooting with Snapshots
docs.text:
If a previously working migration begins producing different results:

  1. Identify the affected target fields.
  2. Review recent Rule History.
  3. Compare the current configuration with a previous snapshot.
  4. Identify changed rules.
  5. Review the associated business requirement.
  6. Test representative records.
  7. Correct the current configuration if necessary.

docs.title: Important Consideration
docs.text:
Snapshots should support controlled rule development, not replace testing.

The preferred workflow remains:

Snapshot
   │
   ▼
Modify
   │
   ▼
Test
   │
   ▼
Validate
   │
   ▼
Approve

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text: Continue to Sync / Merge to understand how Rule Configuration changes can be compared and merged between different copies of the configuration.

docs.title: Sync / Merge Rule Configurations
docs.text:
The Sync / Merge functionality is used to compare two Rule Configuration files and selectively merge changes into the local configuration.

This is useful when multiple users are working on migration rules independently.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
During migration development, two users may modify different copies of the same Rule Configuration.

For example:

Original MMS200MI
       │
       ├───────────────┐
       ▼               ▼
   User A           User B
       │               │
Modify PLCD        Modify PUIT
Modify ORTY        Modify EOQM
       │               │
       └───────┬───────┘
               ▼
          Sync / Merge
               │
               ▼
     Combined Configuration

Sync / Merge provides a controlled method for reviewing those differences before modifying the local Rule Configuration.

docs.title: Accessing Sync / Merge
docs.text:
Navigate to:

Sync / Merge

from the main application.

The Sync / Merge interface allows a local Rule Configuration to be compared with another Rule Configuration.

docs.title: Local and Incoming Configuration
docs.text: The process involves two configurations.

docs.title: Local Configuration
docs.text:
The Rule Configuration currently maintained by the user.

For example:

config/rules/MMS200MI.xlsx

docs.title: Incoming Configuration
docs.text:
Another copy containing changes that may need to be incorporated.

For example:

User B
   │
   ▼
MMS200MI.xlsx

The incoming file should be reviewed before its changes are applied locally.

docs.title: Comparison Process
docs.text:
The application compares the Rule Configurations and identifies differences.

Conceptually:

Local Rules
     │
     │
     ├──── Compare ──── Incoming Rules
     │                       │
     └──────────┬────────────┘
                ▼
           Differences
                │
                ▼
             Review

This is safer than simply replacing the local Rule Configuration with another user's file.

docs.title: What Should Be Compared
docs.text:
Important rule properties include:

TARGET_FIELD
SOURCE_FIELD
RULE_TYPE
RULE_VALUE
SCOPE

For example:

docs.title: Local
docs.text:
TARGET_FIELD = PLCD
SOURCE_FIELD = MBPUIT
RULE_TYPE    = PYTHON
SCOPE        = GLOBAL

docs.title: Incoming
docs.text:
TARGET_FIELD = PLCD
SOURCE_FIELD = MBPUIT
RULE_TYPE    = PYTHON
SCOPE        = DIV_US

Although the target field is the same, the scope is different and should be reviewed carefully.

docs.title: Example Rule Difference
docs.text:
Suppose the local PLCD rule contains:

if puit == "1":
    return "01"

The incoming configuration contains:

if itty in ("SF", "FG") and puit == "1":
    return "02"

Sync / Merge should allow this difference to be identified before the local configuration is changed.

The reviewer should determine:

Which rule represents the approved requirement?

before accepting the incoming change.

docs.title: Selective Merge
docs.text:
Not every incoming change needs to be accepted.

For example:

Incoming Changes

PLCD   ✓ Accept
PUIT   ✓ Accept
ORTY   ✗ Reject
EOQM   ✓ Accept

The purpose of Sync / Merge is to allow changes to be reviewed individually rather than blindly replacing the entire configuration.

docs.title: Conflicting Changes
docs.text:
A conflict can occur when both configurations modify the same rule differently.

Example:

               PLCD
                 │
        ┌────────┴────────┐
        ▼                 ▼
      Local            Incoming
        │                 │
   PLCD = 02          PLCD = 03
        │                 │
        └────────┬────────┘
                 ▼
              Conflict

A conflict requires review.

The correct result should be determined from the approved migration business requirement, not simply from which file is newer.

docs.title: Scope Conflicts
docs.text:
Scope should always be considered during comparison.

These may represent two separate valid rules:

PLCD / GLOBAL
PLCD / DIV_US

while these may represent competing versions:

PLCD / GLOBAL
PLCD / GLOBAL

The combination of:

TARGET_FIELD + SCOPE

is therefore important when reviewing differences.

docs.title: Recommended Merge Workflow
docs.text:
Use the following process when receiving another Rule Configuration:

  1. Identify the incoming Rule Configuration.
  2. Open Sync / Merge.
  3. Compare it with the local configuration.
  4. Review the detected differences.
  5. Identify changed target fields.
  6. Review changes to SOURCE_FIELD.
  7. Review changes to RULE_TYPE.
  8. Review changes to RULE_VALUE.
  9. Review changes to SCOPE.
  10. Select only the approved changes.
  11. Merge them into the local configuration.
  12. Review the resulting Rule Configuration.
  13. Test the affected migrations.

docs.title: After a Merge
docs.text:
A successful merge means:

The selected configuration changes were incorporated.

It does not mean:

The resulting migration output has been validated.

After merging:

Merge
 │
 ▼
Identify Changed Rules
 │
 ▼
Determine Dependencies
 │
 ▼
Load by ID
 │
 ▼
Validate Results
 │
 ▼
Standard Migration
 │
 ▼
Validate Complete Output

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose another user sends an updated MMS200MI Rule Configuration.

The comparison identifies:

Target Field Local Incoming Action ITNO DIRECT DIRECT No change PLCD Python v1 Python v2 Review PUIT DIRECT Python Review ORTY Python v1 Python v1 No change

Only PLCD and PUIT require attention.

After reviewing the requirements, you may decide:

PLCD → Accept Incoming
PUIT → Keep Local

The resulting configuration contains the approved combination of both files.

docs.title: Multiple Users
docs.text:
When several users work on Rule Configurations, avoid workflows such as:

User A edits file
      ↓
User B replaces file
      ↓
User A changes disappear

Instead use:

User A Changes
      │
      ├──────┐
      │      │
User B Changes
      │      │
      └──┬───┘
         ▼
     Compare
         │
         ▼
      Review
         │
         ▼
       Merge

This reduces the risk of accidentally overwriting valid migration logic.

docs.title: Snapshots Before Merge
docs.text:
Before performing a significant merge, preserving the current Rule Configuration is recommended.

Current Configuration
        │
        ▼
     Snapshot
        │
        ▼
   Sync / Merge
        │
        ▼
      Testing

This provides a reference point if unexpected results appear after the merge.

docs.title: Validation After Merge
docs.text:
Focus testing on the fields that changed.

For example:

Changed:

PLCD
PUIT
ORTY

Identify representative records for those rules and test them using Load by ID.

Then perform a Standard Migration to verify the complete output.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If unexpected results appear after a merge:

  1. Identify the affected target field.
  2. Review the current rule.
  3. Review Rule History.
  4. Compare with the pre-merge configuration or snapshot.
  5. Check whether the rule came from the incoming configuration.
  6. Verify the selected scope.
  7. Test representative source records.
  8. Compare expected and actual results.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
Treat Sync / Merge as a review process, not simply a file-copy operation.

The preferred workflow is:

Compare
   │
   ▼
Understand
   │
   ▼
Select
   │
   ▼
Merge
   │
   ▼
Test
   │
   ▼
Validate

Every accepted rule change should have a clear migration or business reason.

docs.title: Rules & Admin Workflow
docs.text:
The administrative features work together:

Rule Development
      │
      ▼
Rule History
      │
      ▼
Snapshots
      │
      ▼
Sync / Merge
      │
      ▼
Testing
      │
      ▼
Validated Configuration

These controls help maintain reliable Rule Configurations as migration development progresses.

docs.title: Business Units and Rule Scope
docs.text:
The Business Unit / Scope functionality allows the Data Migration Tool to apply different transformation rules depending on the organization, division, or migration context being processed.

The default scope is:

GLOBAL

GLOBAL rules define the standard transformation behavior.

When a business unit requires different logic, a more specific scope can override the GLOBAL rule.

docs.title: Why Scope Is Needed
docs.text:
Most transformation rules may be common across the organization.

For example:

ITNO
MBITNO → ITNO

may work the same way everywhere.

However, some M3 fields may require different transformation logic depending on the business unit.

Instead of creating completely separate Rule Configuration files, the Data Migration Tool allows multiple versions of a rule to exist under different scopes.

Conceptually:

                  TARGET_FIELD
                       │
                       ▼
                     PLCD
                       │
             ┌─────────┴─────────┐
             ▼                   ▼
          GLOBAL             DIVISION
           Rule                 Rule
                                 │
                                 ▼
                             Override

docs.title: GLOBAL Scope
docs.text:
GLOBAL represents the default transformation rule.

Example:

TARGET_FIELD SOURCE_FIELD RULE_TYPE SCOPE ITNO MBITNO DIRECT GLOBAL PUIT MBPUIT DIRECT GLOBAL

When the migration is executed using:

Scope = GLOBAL

the GLOBAL rules are used.

docs.title: Business-Specific Scope
docs.text:
A business-specific scope can provide different logic for a target field.

Example:

TARGET_FIELD RULE_TYPE SCOPE PLCD PYTHON GLOBAL PLCD PYTHON DIV_US

In this example, two rules exist for:

PLCD

The GLOBAL rule provides the default logic.

The DIV_US rule provides different logic when that scope is selected.

docs.title: How Overrides Work
docs.text:
When a specific scope is selected, the Data Migration Tool loads:

GLOBAL Rules
      +
Selected Scope Rules

If both contain a rule for the same TARGET_FIELD, the specific scope takes precedence.

For example:

GLOBAL
PLCD → Rule A

DIV_US
PLCD → Rule B

Running:

Scope = GLOBAL

uses:

PLCD → Rule A

Running:

Scope = DIV_US

uses:

PLCD → Rule B

Other GLOBAL fields without a DIV_US override continue using their GLOBAL rules.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Assume the Rule Configuration contains:

TARGET_FIELD RULE_TYPE RULE_VALUE SCOPE CONO CONST 100 GLOBAL ITNO DIRECT GLOBAL PLCD PYTHON Global PLCD logic GLOBAL PLCD PYTHON US PLCD logic DIV_US

When running:

Scope = DIV_US

the effective configuration becomes:

CONO → GLOBAL rule
ITNO → GLOBAL rule
PLCD → DIV_US rule

Only PLCD is overridden.

docs.title: Selecting Scope During Migration
docs.text:
Navigate to:

Run Migration → Standard

The Standard Migration screen includes:

3. Scope (Optional)

The default selection is:

GLOBAL

Configured business units are added to the available options.

For example:

GLOBAL
DIV_US
DIV_CA

Select the appropriate scope before clicking:

RUN MIGRATION

docs.title: Business Unit Configuration
docs.text:
Available business units are loaded from:

config/business_units.csv

The application reads the configured UNIT values and adds them to the Scope dropdown.

Conceptually:

business_units.csv
       │
       ▼
Configured Units
       │
       ▼
Scope Dropdown

docs.title: Scope and Rule Configuration
docs.text:
Scope is stored with the transformation rule.

Example:

TARGET_FIELD = PLCD
SOURCE_FIELD = MBPUIT
RULE_TYPE    = PYTHON
SCOPE        = DIV_US

This means the rule applies when:

DIV_US

is selected for the migration.

docs.title: When to Create an Override
docs.text:
Create a scope-specific rule only when the business requirement actually differs from the GLOBAL rule.

For example:

GLOBAL Requirement

PUIT = 1 → PLCD = 02

Suppose one division requires:

DIV_US Requirement

PUIT = 1 → PLCD = 03

Then an override is appropriate:

PLCD / GLOBAL
        │
        └── Default logic

PLCD / DIV_US
        │
        └── Division-specific logic

docs.title: Avoid Duplicating GLOBAL Rules
docs.text:
Do not create scope-specific copies of every GLOBAL rule when the transformation is identical.

For example, if:

ITNO = MBITNO

works globally, there is no need to create:

ITNO / GLOBAL
ITNO / DIV_US
ITNO / DIV_CA

with identical logic.

Keep:

ITNO / GLOBAL

and create overrides only where required.

This keeps the Rule Configuration easier to maintain.

docs.title: Scope Selection Is Important
docs.text:
Selecting the wrong scope can change the resulting migration values.

For example:

Source
PUIT = 1

GLOBAL Rule
    ↓
PLCD = 02

DIV_US Rule
    ↓
PLCD = 03

The same source record can therefore produce different output depending on the selected scope.

!!! warning Always verify the selected migration scope before generating a production load file.

docs.title: Testing Scope Overrides
docs.text:
When creating an override, test both configurations.

For example:

docs.title: Test 1 — GLOBAL
docs.text:
Scope: GLOBAL
Source PUIT: 1
Expected PLCD: 02

docs.title: Test 2 — DIV_US
docs.text:
Scope: DIV_US
Source PUIT: 1
Expected PLCD: 03

This verifies that:

  1. The GLOBAL rule still works.
  2. The override is applied only to the intended scope.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
When using scopes:

  1. Define the standard transformation as GLOBAL.
  2. Identify genuine business-unit differences.
  3. Create overrides only for those differences.
  4. Keep the same TARGET_FIELD for the overridden rule.
  5. Clearly document why the override exists.
  6. Test both GLOBAL and specific-scope behavior.
  7. Verify the selected scope before production migration.

A good configuration should look conceptually like:

GLOBAL
│
├── ITNO
├── ITTY
├── PUIT
├── PLCD
├── STAT
└── ...

DIV_US
│
└── PLCD      ← Override only

DIV_CA
│
├── PLCD      ← Override
└── STAT      ← Override

Most rules remain GLOBAL while only genuine business differences are overridden.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If a scope-specific rule is not being applied, verify:

  • The business unit exists in config/business_units.csv.
  • The correct scope was selected before running the migration.
  • The Rule Configuration contains the expected SCOPE.
  • The TARGET_FIELD matches the GLOBAL target field being overridden.
  • The scope name matches exactly.
  • The Rule Configuration was saved before running the migration.

If the migration behaves correctly under GLOBAL but incorrectly under another scope, compare the GLOBAL and scope-specific rules for the affected target field.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text: The next configuration topic is Database Configuration, which explains how SQL Server connections are configured when SQL is used as a migration source.

docs.title: Database Configuration
docs.text:
The Data Migration Tool supports SQL Server as a source of legacy migration data.

Instead of loading the source from an Excel or CSV file, a migration can execute a SQL query and use the returned records as the source dataset.

docs.title: SQL Migration Flow
docs.text:
When SQL is configured as the source, the migration flow becomes:

SQL Server
    │
    ▼
SQL Query
    │
    ▼
Data Extractor
    │
    ▼
Source DataFrame
    │
    ▼
FILTER Rules
    │
    ▼
Transformation Rules
    │
    ▼
M3 SDT Output

From the Rule Configuration perspective, the resulting SQL data behaves similarly to data loaded from Excel.

docs.title: Database Configuration File
docs.text:
Database connection information is stored in:

config/db_config.ini

The Data Extractor reads this file when a SQL source is detected.

A configuration follows this general structure:

[DEFAULT]
Driver=ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server
Server=SERVER_NAME
Database=DATABASE_NAME
Trusted_Connection=yes

docs.title: Driver
docs.text:
Driver identifies the ODBC driver used to connect to SQL Server.

Example:

Driver=ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server

The specified driver must be installed on the computer running the Data Migration Tool.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
Server identifies the SQL Server instance.

Example:

Server=SQLSERVER01

Depending on the environment, this may also contain a named instance.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Database identifies the database containing the migration source data.

Example:

Database=LegacyDB

The SQL query configured for the migration will execute against this database.

docs.title: Trusted Connection
docs.text:
The current database configuration supports Windows authentication through:

Trusted_Connection=yes

This means SQL Server uses the Windows credentials of the user running the Data Migration Tool.

Conceptually:

Windows User
     │
     ▼
Data Migration Tool
     │
     ▼
SQL Server Authentication
     │
     ▼
Configured Database

The user must therefore have the required SQL Server permissions.

docs.title: Required Python Libraries
docs.text:
SQL connectivity requires:

sqlalchemy
pyodbc

If these libraries are not installed, SQL sources cannot be loaded.

They can be installed using:

pip install sqlalchemy pyodbc

docs.title: SQL Sources
docs.text:
A source is recognized as SQL when it begins with:

SQL:

Example:

SQL:SELECT * FROM MITMAS

The Data Extractor removes the SQL: prefix and executes:

SELECT * FROM MITMAS

against the configured database.

docs.title: Source Map Example
docs.text:
SQL can be configured directly as the source in the Source Map.

For example:

MCO_SHEET,SOURCE_FILE
Item Master,SQL:SELECT * FROM MITMAS

When Item Master is selected during Standard Migration:

Item Master
     │
     ▼
Source Map
     │
     ▼
SQL:SELECT * FROM MITMAS
     │
     ▼
SQL Server

The returned records become the source dataset used by the migration rules.

docs.title: Using SQL Columns in Rules
docs.text:
Columns returned by the SQL query become available to the Rule Configuration.

For example:

SELECT
    MBITNO,
    MBPUIT,
    MBSTAT
FROM MITMAS

produces source columns:

MBITNO
MBPUIT
MBSTAT

A rule can then use:

TARGET_FIELD = ITNO
SOURCE_FIELD = MBITNO
RULE_TYPE    = DIRECT

A Python rule can also access the returned fields:

itno = str(row.get("MBITNO", "")).strip()
puit = str(row.get("MBPUIT", "")).strip()

docs.title: NULL Values
docs.text:
SQL results may contain NULL values.

The Data Extractor normalizes SQL data after loading it so that null-like values can be handled consistently during transformation.

Rules should still handle blank values when the business requirement requires it.

Example:

value = str(row.get("MBPUIT", "")).strip()

if value == "":
    return ""

return value

docs.title: Database Permissions
docs.text:
The Windows account running the Data Migration Tool must have permission to:

  • Connect to the SQL Server
  • Access the configured database
  • Read the tables or views referenced by the query

For migration extraction, read-only database access is normally sufficient when the configured queries only retrieve source data.

!!! warning SQL queries used as migration sources should be reviewed carefully. The Data Migration Tool executes the SQL text configured after the SQL: prefix.

docs.title: Recommended SQL Queries
docs.text:
Prefer selecting only the fields required for the migration.

Instead of:

SELECT *
FROM MITMAS

consider:

SELECT
    MBITNO,
    MBITTY,
    MBPUIT,
    MBSTAT
FROM MITMAS

This makes the source definition clearer and reduces unnecessary data retrieval.

When appropriate, SQL can also restrict the migration population:

SELECT
    MBITNO,
    MBITTY,
    MBPUIT,
    MBSTAT
FROM MITMAS
WHERE MBCONO = 100

docs.title: SQL Filtering vs FILTER Rules
docs.text:
SQL conditions and Data Migration Tool FILTER rules can both restrict the source population, but they operate at different stages.

SQL Server
    │
    │ WHERE condition
    ▼
Extracted Dataset
    │
    │ FILTER rule
    ▼
Migration Dataset

A SQL WHERE clause limits which records are extracted from the database.

A FILTER rule limits which extracted records continue through the migration process.

The migration design should clearly identify where population-selection logic belongs.

docs.title: Testing the Connection
docs.text:
Before using a SQL source for migration, verify:

  1. The ODBC driver is installed.
  2. db_config.ini exists.
  3. The server name is correct.
  4. The database name is correct.
  5. Windows authentication is permitted.
  6. The user has access to the database.
  7. sqlalchemy and pyodbc are installed.
  8. The SQL query executes successfully.
  9. The returned columns match the Rule Configuration.

docs.title: SQLAlchemy or pyodbc Not Installed
docs.text:
The application may report that SQL support is unavailable.

Install:

pip install sqlalchemy pyodbc

docs.title: Database Configuration Not Found
docs.text:
Verify that the following file exists:

config/db_config.ini

docs.title: Login or Permission Error
docs.text: Verify that the Windows user running the application has access to the configured SQL Server and database.

docs.title: Invalid Object Name
docs.text:
If SQL Server reports an invalid table or view, verify:

  • Database
  • Schema
  • Table name
  • View name

For example, the fully qualified object may need to be:

dbo.MITMAS

instead of:

MITMAS

depending on the database configuration.

docs.title: Missing Source Field
docs.text:
If the migration runs but a rule returns blank values, verify that the SQL query actually returns the field expected by SOURCE_FIELD.

For example:

Rule expects:

MBPUIT

but the query only returns:

SELECT MBITNO, MBSTAT
FROM MITMAS

MBPUIT will not be available to the transformation rule.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Database configuration should be treated as environment-specific configuration.

Avoid placing passwords or other sensitive credentials directly inside Rule Configuration files or SQL queries.

The current trusted-connection configuration allows Windows authentication to be used without storing a database password in the migration rule.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
For SQL-based migrations:

  1. Configure the SQL Server connection.
  2. Test database connectivity.
  3. Create a focused source query.
  4. Verify the returned columns.
  5. Add the SQL source to the Source Map.
  6. Verify the Rule Configuration dependencies.
  7. Run a small test migration.
  8. Compare the SQL source records with the generated SDT.
  9. Validate record counts and transformed values before production migration.

The complete relationship becomes:

db_config.ini
      │
      ▼
SQL Server
      │
      ▼
SQL Query
      │
      ▼
Source Map
      │
      ▼
Rule Configuration
      │
      ▼
SDT Output

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text: With the core configuration documented, the next section covers Run Migration, including the different migration methods available in the Data Migration Tool.

docs.title: MCO Import
docs.text:
The MCO Import function is used to create or update migration configuration from an MCO workbook.

The MCO provides the field-level information required to establish the relationship between legacy source fields and the corresponding M3 target fields.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
When preparing a new migration object, the MCO acts as one of the primary specifications for the migration.

The import process helps convert information from the MCO into configuration that can be used by the Data Migration Tool.

Conceptually:

MCO Workbook
     │
     ▼
MCO Import
     │
     ▼
Analyze MCO Fields
     │
     ▼
Migration Configuration
     │
     ├── Target Fields
     ├── Source Fields
     └── Initial Rule Information

This reduces the need to manually create the initial Rule Configuration from scratch.

docs.title: Accessing MCO Import
docs.text:
From the application, navigate to:

Configuration → Import MCO

Select the MCO workbook that contains the migration specification.

docs.title: MCO Workbook
docs.text:
An MCO workbook may contain multiple worksheets representing different migration objects.

For example:

MCO Workbook
│
├── Item Master
├── Item Facility
├── Item Warehouse
├── Supplier
└── Customer

Each worksheet can contain information about the source and target fields required for that migration object.

docs.title: Field Identification
docs.text:
During MCO processing, the tool looks for information identifying the M3 target field and the corresponding legacy source field.

For example:

M3 Field       Source
--------       --------
ITNO           MBITNO
ITTY           MMITTY
PUIT           MBPUIT

This information provides the foundation for creating transformation rules.

docs.title: Source Field Prefixes
docs.text:
Legacy Movex fields frequently contain prefixes that identify the source table or business object.

For example:

MBITNO
MMITTY
OKCUNO
IDSUNO

The application can analyze these field names and learn source prefixes.

Example:

MB → Item-related source
MM → Item-related source
OK → Customer-related source

These signatures can later assist features such as Auto-Detect Migration.

docs.title: API Identification
docs.text:
When API information is available in the MCO, the tool can identify M3 API names using patterns such as:

MMS200MI
CRS610MI
CRS620MI

This information helps establish the relationship:

MCO Business Object
        │
        ▼
      M3 API
        │
        ▼
Rule Configuration

docs.title: Rule Configuration
docs.text:
The MCO provides the starting point for creating transformation rules.

However, importing the MCO does not mean that all migration rules are complete.

Some fields may require:

DIRECT
CONST
MAP
PYTHON
FILTER

depending on the business requirement.

For example, an MCO may establish:

TARGET_FIELD = ITNO
SOURCE_FIELD = MBITNO

A simple field may then use:

RULE_TYPE = DIRECT

But another field such as:

PLCD

may depend on several source fields and require a PYTHON rule.

docs.title: MCO Import vs Rule Development
docs.text:
These are two separate activities.

MCO Import
    │
    ▼
Initial Configuration
    │
    ▼
Rule Review
    │
    ▼
Business Logic Development
    │
    ▼
Testing
    │
    ▼
Approved Rule Configuration

!!! important MCO Import should be considered the starting point of Rule Configuration, not the end of rule development.

Rules must still be reviewed against the approved migration requirements.

docs.title: After Importing an MCO
docs.text:
After the import process is complete:

  1. Review the generated migration configuration.
  2. Verify the M3 target fields.
  3. Verify the identified source fields.
  4. Confirm the associated M3 API.
  5. Review the generated Rule Configuration.
  6. Identify fields requiring additional business logic.
  7. Create any required MAP or PYTHON rules.
  8. Configure the source and migration mappings.
  9. Run a test migration.
  10. Validate the generated SDT output.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose the MCO contains:

M3 FIELD     SOURCE
--------     -------
ITNO         MBITNO
PUIT         MBPUIT

The initial configuration may establish:

ITNO ← MBITNO
PUIT ← MBPUIT

For ITNO, a direct transformation may be sufficient:

TARGET_FIELD = ITNO
SOURCE_FIELD = MBITNO
RULE_TYPE    = DIRECT

For another target field, the MCO information may only provide part of what is required.

The migration team must then add the appropriate business transformation logic.

docs.title: Relationship with Auto-Detect
docs.text:
The Data Migration Tool can also analyze MCO worksheets to learn field signatures.

For example:

MMITTY

produces the prefix:

MM

When a legacy file is later analyzed, the Auto-Detect process can compare its headers against known MCO prefixes.

Conceptually:

MCO
 │
 ▼
Learn Prefixes
 │
 ▼
MM → Item Master
OK → Customer
ID → Supplier
 │
 ▼
Legacy File Headers
 │
 ▼
Identify Migration Object

This allows the application to assist with identifying the appropriate migration configuration automatically.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
After MCO Import, verify that:

  • The correct MCO worksheet was processed.
  • Target fields correspond to the expected M3 fields.
  • Source fields correspond to the correct legacy fields.
  • The correct API is associated with the migration object.
  • Rule Configuration was created correctly.
  • Fields requiring custom business logic have been identified.

The MCO provides the migration specification, while the Rule Configuration defines how that specification is executed by the Data Migration Tool.

docs.title: Migration Map
docs.text:
The Migration Map defines the relationship between a migration business object and the M3 configuration required to generate its output.

While the Source Map determines where the legacy data comes from, the Migration Map determines where that data is going and which M3 structure should be used.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Migration Map connects the major M3 components of a migration:

MCO Business Object
        │
        ▼
   Migration Map
        │
        ├── M3 API
        │
        ├── SDT Template
        │
        └── Transaction Sheet(s)

This allows the Data Migration Tool to automatically resolve the correct output configuration during migration.

docs.title: Migration Map File
docs.text:
The Migration Map is stored in:

config/migration_map.csv

The Migration Runner reads this file when determining the API, SDT template, and transaction sheets associated with a migration.

docs.title: Main Fields
docs.text:
The current Migration Map uses the following key fields:

Field Purpose MCO_SHEET Identifies the migration business object API_NAME Identifies the M3 API / Rule Configuration SDT_TEMPLATE Identifies the SDT workbook used for output TRANSACTION_SHEET Identifies the SDT sheet or sheets to populate

docs.title: MCO_SHEET
docs.text:
MCO_SHEET identifies the business object from the MCO.

Examples may include:

Item Master
Item Facility
Item Warehouse
Supplier
Customer

This is an important lookup key because multiple migration objects may use related APIs but require different SDT configurations.

For example:

Item Master
      │
      ▼
Migration Map

The tool can then resolve the exact configuration associated with Item Master.

docs.title: API_NAME
docs.text:
API_NAME identifies the M3 API associated with the migration.

Example:

MMS200MI

The API is also associated with the Rule Configuration used by the migration.

For example:

MCO Sheet
   │
   ▼
Item Master
   │
   ▼
MMS200MI
   │
   ▼
config/rules/MMS200MI.xlsx

docs.title: SDT_TEMPLATE
docs.text:
SDT_TEMPLATE identifies the M3 SDT workbook that should be used to generate the migration output.

SDT templates are normally stored under:

config/sdt_templates/

For example:

config/sdt_templates/MMS200MI.xlsx

The template provides the required M3 workbook structure.

The Data Migration Tool does not create the SDT structure from scratch during each migration. Instead, it populates the appropriate fields in the configured template.

docs.title: TRANSACTION_SHEET
docs.text:
TRANSACTION_SHEET identifies the SDT worksheet or worksheets that should receive the transformed data.

A migration may require one transaction sheet:

AddItemBasic

or multiple transaction sheets:

AddItemBasic,UpdItemBasic

Multiple transaction sheets are stored as a comma-separated list.

The Migration Runner converts this value into the list of sheets that should be processed.

docs.title: Complete Relationship
docs.text:
A Migration Map entry can be understood as:

MCO_SHEET
    │
    ▼
Business Object
    │
    ├── API_NAME
    │
    ├── SDT_TEMPLATE
    │
    └── TRANSACTION_SHEET

For example:

Item Master
    │
    ├── MMS200MI
    ├── MMS200MI SDT Template
    └── Required Transaction Sheet(s)

docs.title: Relationship with Source Map
docs.text:
The Source Map and Migration Map work together.

                   MCO_SHEET
                       │
            ┌──────────┴──────────┐
            │                     │
            ▼                     ▼
       Source Map            Migration Map
            │                     │
            ▼                     ├── API
      Legacy Source               ├── SDT Template
                                  └── Transaction Sheets
            │                     │
            └──────────┬──────────┘
                       ▼
                 Migration Runner

The Source Map answers:

Where does the data come from?

The Migration Map answers:

Which M3 configuration should process it?

docs.title: Relationship with Rules
docs.text:
The API resolved through the Migration Map is connected to the Rule Configuration.

For example:

MCO_SHEET
    │
    ▼
Item Master
    │
    ▼
API_NAME
    │
    ▼
MMS200MI
    │
    ▼
Rule Configuration
    │
    ▼
config/rules/MMS200MI.xlsx

The Rule Configuration then determines how each source field is transformed.

docs.title: Standard Migration Flow
docs.text:
When Standard Migration is executed, the process can be represented as:

User selects MCO Source
        │
        ▼
Resolve Source Map
        │
        ▼
Load Legacy Source
        │
        ▼
Resolve Migration Map
        │
        ├── API
        ├── SDT Template
        └── Transaction Sheets
        │
        ▼
Load Rule Configuration
        │
        ▼
Apply Transformation Rules
        │
        ▼
Generate SDT Output

docs.title: Why MCO_SHEET Is Important
docs.text:
The Data Migration Tool can resolve migration information using MCO_SHEET.

This is important because using only the API name may be ambiguous.

For example, two MCO business objects could potentially reference the same API but require different migration definitions.

Conceptually:

Business Object A ──┐
                    ├── Same API
Business Object B ──┘

But they may require:

Different SDT Templates
or
Different Transaction Sheets

Using the MCO context allows the application to select the configuration belonging to the actual business object.

docs.title: SDT Template Resolution
docs.text:
During migration, the application first attempts to resolve the configured SDT template from the Migration Map.

If the configured template exists under:

config/sdt_templates/

that template is used.

The Migration Runner also contains fallback logic that can search for a template beginning with the API name.

However, the preferred configuration is an explicit Migration Map entry.

!!! tip Maintain the Migration Map correctly rather than relying on fallback template detection.

docs.title: Example Migration Map
docs.text:
A simplified configuration could look like:

MCO_SHEET,API_NAME,SDT_TEMPLATE,TRANSACTION_SHEET
Item Master,MMS200MI,MMS200MI.xlsx,AddItemBasic

This means:

Item Master
     │
     ├── API: MMS200MI
     │
     ├── Template: MMS200MI.xlsx
     │
     └── Sheet: AddItemBasic

When Item Master is selected, the application has the information required to determine the M3 output configuration.

docs.title: Multiple Transaction Sheets
docs.text:
Some migrations require more than one SDT transaction sheet.

Example:

TRANSACTION_SHEET
AddItemBasic,UpdItemBasic

The application separates the value by commas:

AddItemBasic
UpdItemBasic

and processes the required sheets.

This allows one migration configuration to populate multiple sections of an SDT workbook when required.

docs.title: Creating a New Migration Map Entry
docs.text:
When configuring a new migration object:

  1. Identify the MCO business object.
  2. Identify the M3 API.
  3. Identify the correct SDT template.
  4. Identify the required transaction sheet or sheets.
  5. Add the configuration to migration_map.csv.
  6. Verify that the SDT template exists.
  7. Verify that the corresponding Rule Configuration exists.
  8. Test the migration.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Before running a production migration, verify the complete relationship:

MCO Sheet
    ↓
Source Map
    ↓
Correct Legacy Source

MCO Sheet
    ↓
Migration Map
    ↓
Correct API
    ↓
Correct Rule Configuration
    ↓
Correct SDT Template
    ↓
Correct Transaction Sheet(s)

A mistake in the Migration Map can cause the migration to use the wrong M3 structure even when the transformation rules themselves are correct.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If the migration cannot determine the SDT template, verify:

  • config/migration_map.csv exists.
  • MCO_SHEET matches the selected business object.
  • API_NAME is correct.
  • SDT_TEMPLATE contains the correct filename.
  • The template exists under config/sdt_templates/.
  • TRANSACTION_SHEET contains valid SDT worksheet names.

If the wrong migration configuration is selected, verify the MCO_SHEET relationship first.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
Treat MCO_SHEET as the business-object identity connecting the migration configuration.

A well-defined configuration should make this relationship clear:

MCO Business Object
        │
        ├── Source
        ├── API
        ├── Rules
        ├── SDT Template
        └── Transaction Sheets

This provides a consistent and repeatable migration setup.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text: After configuring the Migration Map, review Business Units and Scope to understand how GLOBAL rules and business-specific overrides are applied.

docs.title: Configuration Overview
docs.text:
The Configuration area defines how the Data Migration Tool connects legacy source data with the appropriate M3 migration configuration.

Configuration provides the information the application needs to determine:

  • Where the source data comes from
  • Which MCO business object is being migrated
  • Which M3 API is associated with the migration
  • Which Rule Configuration should be used
  • Which SDT template should receive the transformed data
  • Which transaction sheets are required

docs.title: Configuration in the Migration Process
docs.text:
Configuration connects the major components of a migration.

Legacy Source
      │
      ▼
Source Configuration
      │
      ▼
MCO / Business Object
      │
      ├─────────────► Rule Configuration
      │
      ▼
M3 API
      │
      ▼
SDT Template
      │
      ▼
Transaction Sheet(s)
      │
      ▼
Migration Output

Without the correct configuration, the application may not be able to determine which source, rules, API, or SDT template should be used.

docs.title: Main Configuration Components
docs.text: The Data Migration Tool uses several configuration components.

docs.title: MCO Specification
docs.text:
The MCO specification provides information about the migration business objects and their source-to-target field relationships.

The tool can analyze an MCO workbook and use that information to help create migration configurations.

docs.title: Source Map
docs.text:
The Source Map defines where the legacy data for a migration comes from.

It connects an MCO sheet or business object with its corresponding source.

The source may be:

  • Excel
  • CSV
  • SQL

Conceptually:

MCO Sheet
    │
    ▼
Source Map
    │
    ▼
Legacy Source

docs.title: Migration Map
docs.text:
The Migration Map connects the migration business object with the M3 configuration required to generate the output.

It can identify information such as:

MCO Sheet
    │
    ├──► API
    ├──► SDT Template
    └──► Transaction Sheet(s)

This allows the Migration Runner to automatically determine which SDT structure should be used.

docs.title: Rule Configuration
docs.text:
The Rule Configuration contains the transformation logic.

For example:

Legacy Source
      │
      ▼
Rule Configuration
      │
      ▼
M3 Target Values

Rule Configuration files are normally stored under:

config/rules/

See Understanding the Rule Configuration for more information.

docs.title: SDT Templates
docs.text:
SDT templates define the M3 output structure.

Templates are normally stored under:

config/sdt_templates/

The Migration Map determines which template should be associated with a migration.

docs.title: Business Units and Scope
docs.text:
Business-unit configuration allows transformation rules to vary when required.

The default rule scope is:

GLOBAL

Additional scopes can be configured for business-specific requirements.

For example:

GLOBAL
DIV_US
DIV_CA

docs.title: Database Configuration
docs.text:
The Data Migration Tool can also use SQL as a source.

Database connection information is maintained separately from the transformation rules.

A SQL source can then be used by the extraction process instead of an Excel or CSV file.

docs.title: Why Configuration Matters
docs.text:
Consider a migration for Item Master.

The tool needs to understand the complete relationship:

Item Master
    │
    ├── Where is the source data?
    │
    ├── Which M3 API applies?
    │
    ├── Which rules should be used?
    │
    ├── Which SDT template applies?
    │
    └── Which transaction sheets should be populated?

Configuration provides these relationships so they do not need to be manually specified every time a migration is executed.

docs.title: Configuration vs Rules
docs.text:
Configuration and Rules serve different purposes.

Configuration Rules Determines what migration setup to use Determines how data is transformed Identifies source Reads source values Identifies API Calculates M3 values Identifies SDT template Applies business logic Identifies transaction sheets Populates target fields

Both are required for a successful migration.

Configuration
      +
Rules
      +
Source Data
      │
      ▼
Migration Engine
      │
      ▼
M3 SDT Output

docs.title: Recommended Configuration Workflow
docs.text:
When preparing a new migration object:

  1. Review the MCO specification.
  2. Identify the legacy source.
  3. Configure the Source Map.
  4. Identify the M3 API.
  5. Configure the Migration Map.
  6. Verify the SDT template.
  7. Create or import the Rule Configuration.
  8. Review transformation rules.
  9. Test the migration.
  10. Validate the generated output.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Continue with:

  • MCO Import
  • Source Map
  • Migration Map
  • Database Configuration

docs.title: Source Map
docs.text:
The Source Map defines where the Data Migration Tool obtains the legacy data for each migration business object.

It connects an MCO business object or worksheet with the source that contains the data to be migrated.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The Source Map answers a fundamental question:

Where does the source data for this migration come from?

Conceptually:

MCO Business Object
        │
        ▼
    Source Map
        │
        ▼
   Source Location
        │
        ▼
Legacy Migration Data

This allows the migration process to use a predefined source instead of requiring the user to manually locate the source every time.

docs.title: Source Map File
docs.text:
The Source Map is stored in:

config/source_map.csv

The Data Migration Tool reads this configuration when displaying available sources in the Standard Migration screen.

docs.title: MCO_SHEET
docs.text:
MCO_SHEET identifies the migration business object.

For example:

Item Master
Item Facility
Item Warehouse
Supplier
Customer

The value should correspond to the MCO business object being configured.

Conceptually:

MCO_SHEET
    │
    ▼
Item Master

The application uses this value to locate the associated source.

docs.title: SOURCE_FILE
docs.text:
SOURCE_FILE identifies where the legacy data should be obtained.

Depending on the migration configuration, this may represent a file or a SQL source.

Example:

MCO_SHEET, SOURCE_FILE
Item Master, raw_data/ItemMaster.xlsx

This tells the Data Migration Tool:

Item Master
     │
     ▼
raw_data/ItemMaster.xlsx

docs.title: File Sources
docs.text:
A source can point to a legacy Excel or CSV file.

For example:

raw_data/ItemMaster.xlsx

or:

raw_data/ItemMaster.csv

During migration, the Data Extractor loads the configured source into the migration process.

The source columns then become available to the Rule Configuration.

Example:

Legacy File
│
├── MBITNO
├── MBPUIT
├── MBSTAT
└── ...
       │
       ▼
Transformation Rules

docs.title: SQL Sources
docs.text:
The Data Migration Tool also supports SQL as a source.

A SQL source is identified using the prefix:

SQL:

For example:

SQL:SELECT * FROM MITMAS

The application recognizes the SQL: prefix and executes the remaining text as a SQL query.

Conceptually:

SOURCE_FILE
     │
     ▼
SQL:SELECT ...
     │
     ▼
SQL Server
     │
     ▼
DataFrame
     │
     ▼
Migration Rules

!!! important SQL sources require the database connection to be configured correctly before the migration can run.

docs.title: Source Selection in Standard Migration
docs.text:
When the user opens:

Run Migration → Standard

the Select Source Data dropdown is populated using the MCO sheets defined in:

config/source_map.csv

For example:

Select Source Data:

Item Master
Item Facility
Item Warehouse
Supplier

When the user selects:

Item Master

the application searches the Source Map for that MCO_SHEET and retrieves its SOURCE_FILE.

The user therefore selects the business object, while the application resolves the actual source location.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Consider this Source Map:

MCO_SHEET,SOURCE_FILE
Item Master,raw_data/ItemMaster.xlsx
Item Facility,raw_data/ItemFacility.xlsx
Supplier,SQL:SELECT * FROM CIDMAS

Selecting:

Item Master

resolves to:

raw_data/ItemMaster.xlsx

Selecting:

Supplier

resolves to:

SQL:SELECT * FROM CIDMAS

docs.title: Relationship with the Rule Configuration
docs.text:
The Source Map determines where the data comes from.

The Rule Configuration determines what happens to the data.

Source Map
    │
    ▼
Legacy Source Data
    │
    ▼
Rule Configuration
    │
    ▼
Transformed M3 Data

For example:

Source Map
    ↓
Item Master → ItemMaster.xlsx

Source Data
    ↓
MBITNO = AP32508

Rule
    ↓
TARGET_FIELD = ITNO
SOURCE_FIELD = MBITNO
RULE_TYPE = DIRECT

Output
    ↓
ITNO = AP32508

docs.title: Relationship with the Migration Map
docs.text:
The Source Map and Migration Map perform different functions.

                 MCO Sheet
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
     Source Map          Migration Map
          │                   │
          ▼                   ├── API
    Legacy Source             ├── SDT Template
                              └── Transaction Sheets

Together they provide the information required to execute the migration.

docs.title: Source Field Names
docs.text:
The source data must contain the columns expected by the Rule Configuration.

For example, if a rule contains:

SOURCE_FIELD = MBPUIT

the selected source should contain:

MBPUIT

If the rule expects one field but the source contains a different field name, the transformation may return a blank or incorrect value.

!!! warning Always verify that the Source Map points to the correct dataset before troubleshooting transformation rules.

docs.title: Updating the Source Map
docs.text:
When configuring a new migration object:

  1. Identify the MCO business object.
  2. Identify the legacy source.
  3. Add the business object to MCO_SHEET.
  4. Define the source in SOURCE_FILE.
  5. Save the Source Map.
  6. Refresh the source list in Standard Migration.
  7. Confirm the new business object appears.
  8. Test that the source can be loaded.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If a source does not appear in Standard Migration, verify:

  • config/source_map.csv exists.
  • The MCO_SHEET column exists.
  • The business object has been added to the Source Map.
  • The CSV file was saved correctly.

If the source appears but the migration cannot load it, verify:

  • SOURCE_FILE contains the correct location.
  • The source file exists.
  • The file is accessible.
  • The SQL configuration is correct when using SQL:.
  • The SQL query is valid.
  • The expected source columns exist.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
The Source Map should represent the approved source for each migration object.

Avoid maintaining multiple ambiguous entries for the same MCO business object unless the migration design specifically requires them.

Before running a migration, the relationship should be clear:

Business Object
      │
      ▼
Approved Source
      │
      ▼
Rule Configuration
      │
      ▼
M3 Output

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text:
After defining the source, configure the Migration Map.

The Migration Map determines which M3 API, SDT template, and transaction sheets are associated with the business object.

docs.title: Standard Migration
docs.text:
Standard Migration is used to execute a migration using an existing Rule Configuration and a source that has already been defined in the application's configuration.

This is the primary migration method when the source, M3 API, transformation rules, and SDT template are already configured.

docs.title: Standard Migration Screen
docs.text:
Navigate to:

Run Migration → Standard

The Standard Migration screen contains three main selections:

  1. Rule Configuration
  2. Source Data
  3. Scope

After these selections have been made, the migration can be started using RUN MIGRATION.

docs.title: 1. Select Rule Configuration
docs.text:
Select the Rule Configuration that should be used for the migration.

Example:

MMS200MI

Rule Configuration files are stored in:

config/rules/

For example:

config/rules/MMS200MI.xlsx

The selected configuration determines the transformation rules that will be applied to the source data.

docs.title: 2. Select Source Data
docs.text:
Select the source dataset from the Source Data dropdown.

The available sources are obtained from:

config/source_map.csv

The selected entry identifies the source associated with an MCO sheet.

The source may point to a file or another configured source such as SQL.

!!! note The source must already exist in the Source Map before it can be selected from Standard Migration.

docs.title: 3. Select Scope
docs.text:
The default scope is:

GLOBAL

A different scope can be selected when business-unit-specific transformation rules are required.

For example:

GLOBAL
DIV_US
DIV_CA

When a specific scope is selected, the Rule Configuration loader determines which rules apply to that scope.

Specific scope rules can override GLOBAL rules for the same target field.

docs.title: 4. Run Migration
docs.text:
After selecting the Rule Configuration, source data, and scope, click:

RUN MIGRATION

The application starts the migration process.

A simplified execution flow is:

Selected Source
      │
      ▼
Load Source Data
      │
      ▼
Load Rule Configuration
      │
      ▼
Apply Filters
      │
      ▼
Apply Transformation Rules
      │
      ▼
Resolve SDT Template
      │
      ▼
Generate Output File

Progress and errors are displayed in the System Log at the bottom of the application.

docs.title: SDT Template Resolution
docs.text:
The application uses the migration configuration to determine which SDT template and transaction sheets are required.

SDT templates are normally located under:

config/sdt_templates/

The relationship between the source, API, SDT template, and transaction sheets is controlled by the migration configuration.

docs.title: Output File
docs.text:
Generated migration files are written to:

output/

A typical automatically generated filename follows a structure similar to:

LOAD_MMS200MI_20260819.xlsx

If a file with the same name already exists, the application can generate a versioned filename such as:

LOAD_MMS200MI_20260819_v1.xlsx

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Assume the following configuration:

Rule Configuration: MMS200MI
Source Data:       Item Master
Scope:             GLOBAL

The application will:

  1. Locate the configured source for Item Master.
  2. Resolve the migration mapping associated with that source.
  3. Load the MMS200MI Rule Configuration.
  4. Load the legacy source data.
  5. Apply configured filters and transformation rules.
  6. Determine the appropriate SDT template and transaction sheets.
  7. Generate the resulting M3 load file in the output directory.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If the migration does not run, verify:

  • A valid Rule Configuration is selected.
  • The source exists in config/source_map.csv.
  • The corresponding migration mapping exists.
  • The Rule Configuration file exists.
  • The required SDT template exists.
  • The source file or SQL source is accessible.

Check the System Log for detailed messages generated during processing.

docs.title: Data Migration Tool Overview
docs.text:
The Data Migration Tool is a Python-based application designed to support the transformation of legacy data into formats required for migration into Infor M3.

The tool provides a graphical interface for configuring migration processes, applying transformation rules, generating M3 SDT files, and managing migration configurations.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
During a data migration, source data does not always match the structure or values expected by M3.

The Data Migration Tool provides a configurable transformation layer between the legacy source data and the M3 target format.

A simplified migration flow is:

Legacy Source Data
        │
        ▼
Rule Configuration
        │
        ▼
Transformation Engine
        │
        ▼
SDT Template
        │
        ▼
M3 Load File

Instead of hard-coding every migration transformation into the application, transformation logic can be maintained through Rule Configuration files.

docs.title: Main Application Areas
docs.text: The application is organized into five main areas.

docs.title: Run Migration
docs.text:
The Run Migration area is used to execute migration processes.

The available migration methods include:

  • Standard Migration
  • Auto-Detect
  • Load by ID
  • Batch Migration

Each method provides a different way of selecting and processing source data.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The Configuration area contains tools used to prepare and maintain the migration environment.

Configuration includes items such as:

  • MCO specifications
  • Source mappings
  • Migration mappings
  • Business units
  • Database configuration
  • Rule configuration generation

docs.title: Rules & Admin
docs.text:
The Rules & Admin area is used to maintain the transformation logic used during migration.

Rule configurations determine how source fields are converted into M3 target fields.

For example:

Source Data

MBITNO = AP32508
MBPUIT = 1
MMITTY = FG

        │
        ▼

Transformation Rules

        │
        ▼

M3 Output

ITNO = AP32508
PUIT = 1
PLCD = 02

Rules may perform direct mappings, assign constants, perform lookups, apply filters, or execute custom Python logic.

docs.title: Utilities
docs.text:
The Utilities area provides supporting tools for migration activities.

Current utilities include:

  • Copy Sheet
  • Merge Files
  • Script Library

These tools can be used independently from the main migration process.

docs.title: Sync / Merge
docs.text:
The Sync / Merge area allows Rule Configuration changes from another user or file to be compared with the local configuration.

Detected differences can be reviewed before selected changes are merged into the local Rule Configuration.

docs.title: Migration Components
docs.text: Several components work together during a migration.

docs.title: Source Data
docs.text:
The source data contains the legacy information that needs to be migrated.

Sources may include Excel or CSV files, and configured processes may also use SQL data sources.

docs.title: Rule Configuration
docs.text:
The Rule Configuration defines how source data should be transformed.

A rule normally identifies:

  • Target field
  • Source field
  • Rule type
  • Rule value or transformation logic
  • Scope

docs.title: SDT Template
docs.text:
The SDT template defines the M3 structure that must be populated.

The tool applies the configured transformation rules and writes the resulting values into the appropriate SDT transaction sheets.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: The result of the migration process is an M3 load file generated in the required SDT structure.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text: Continue to Standard Migration to learn how to execute a standard migration.

docs.title: Auto-Detect Migration
docs.text:
The Auto-Detect Migration function analyzes a legacy source file and attempts to determine which migration business object and configuration should be used.

This is useful when the user has a source file but does not already know which MCO migration object it belongs to.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
In Standard Migration, the user already knows the migration configuration:

User
 │
 ├── Select Rule Configuration
 ├── Select Source
 └── Select Scope

Auto-Detect changes the beginning of this process.

Instead of manually identifying the migration object, the application analyzes the source file structure.

Legacy Source File
        │
        ▼
Analyze Column Headers
        │
        ▼
Compare with Known MCO Signatures
        │
        ▼
Identify Migration Object
        │
        ▼
Resolve Migration Configuration
        │
        ▼
Run Migration

docs.title: How Auto-Detect Works
docs.text:
The Data Migration Tool learns source-field signatures from the configured MCO workbook.

Legacy fields frequently contain prefixes identifying their source table.

For example:

MBITNO
MBPUIT
MBSTAT

share the prefix:

MB

Another source may contain:

MMITNO
MMITTY

with the prefix:

MM

The Auto-Detect process uses these patterns to help identify the migration object.

docs.title: MCO Signatures
docs.text:
During MCO analysis, the application examines source-field definitions and extracts recognizable prefixes.

Conceptually:

MCO
 │
 ├── Item Master
 │      ├── MBITNO
 │      ├── MBPUIT
 │      └── MBSTAT
 │
 ├── Item Facility
 │      ├── MMITNO
 │      └── MMITTY
 │
 ▼
Known Signatures

Item Master    → MB
Item Facility  → MM

These signatures can then be compared against an unknown legacy source file.

docs.title: Source File Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose a source file contains:

MBITNO
MBITTY
MBPUIT
MBSTAT
MBCONO

The application analyzes the column headers and extracts their prefixes.

In this example:

MB

appears repeatedly.

The Auto-Detect process compares that information with the known MCO signatures.

Source File
    │
    ▼
MBITNO
MBITTY
MBPUIT
MBSTAT
    │
    ▼
Detected Prefix
    │
    ▼
MB
    │
    ▼
Known MCO Signatures
    │
    ▼
Potential Migration Match

docs.title: API Detection
docs.text:
The MCO analysis can also identify M3 API names when they are available in the MCO specification.

Examples include:

MMS200MI
CRS610MI
CRS620MI

This information helps connect the detected business object with the appropriate migration configuration.

docs.title: Running Auto-Detect
docs.text:
Navigate to:

Run Migration → Auto-Detect

Select the legacy source file that should be analyzed.

The application will inspect the file headers and compare them against the known migration signatures.

docs.title: Detection Result
docs.text:
When a suitable match is identified, the application can use the detected MCO context to resolve the corresponding migration configuration.

Conceptually:

Legacy File
    │
    ▼
Auto-Detect
    │
    ▼
MCO Business Object
    │
    ▼
Migration Map
    │
    ├── API
    ├── SDT Template
    └── Transaction Sheets
    │
    ▼
Rule Configuration

The normal migration process can then continue.

docs.title: Auto-Detect Does Not Replace Rules
docs.text:
Auto-Detect determines which migration configuration should be used.

It does not determine the business transformation logic for individual target fields.

For example:

Auto-Detect
    │
    ▼
"This appears to be Item Master"
    │
    ▼
MMS200MI Rule Configuration
    │
    ▼
DIRECT / CONST / MAP / PYTHON Rules

The Rule Configuration remains responsible for transforming the source data.

!!! important Auto-Detect helps identify the migration object. It does not replace a complete and validated Rule Configuration.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose the user receives:

Legacy_Item_Data.xlsx

The user may not know which configured migration should process the file.

The file contains:

MBITNO
MBITTY
MBPUIT
MBSTAT

Auto-Detect analyzes the headers:

MBITNO ─┐
MBITTY ─┤
MBPUIT ─┼──► MB
MBSTAT ─┘

The application compares:

MB

against its known MCO signatures.

If a matching migration object is identified, that information can be used to determine the corresponding API and migration configuration.

docs.title: Why Auto-Detect Is Useful
docs.text:
Auto-Detect is particularly useful when:

  • The source filename does not clearly identify the migration object.
  • Multiple migration files are being reviewed.
  • The user is unfamiliar with the legacy source tables.
  • Source files use recognizable Movex field prefixes.
  • The migration configuration has already been established.

Instead of relying only on filenames, the application analyzes the actual source structure.

docs.title: Detection Depends on Configuration
docs.text:
Auto-Detect relies on information learned from the MCO configuration.

Therefore, detection quality depends on the available MCO signatures.

If a migration object has not been configured correctly, Auto-Detect may not be able to identify it.

Good MCO Configuration
        │
        ▼
Good Signatures
        │
        ▼
Better Detection

docs.title: Ambiguous Matches
docs.text:
Some source files may contain fields associated with multiple source tables.

For example:

MBITNO
MBPUIT
MMITNO
MMITTY

In this situation, more than one migration object may appear relevant.

Auto-Detect should therefore be treated as an identification aid rather than a replacement for migration validation.

Always confirm that the detected migration object matches the intended business requirement.

docs.title: Validation Before Migration
docs.text:
After Auto-Detect identifies a migration configuration, verify:

  1. The detected MCO business object is correct.
  2. The expected API is selected.
  3. The correct Rule Configuration exists.
  4. The correct SDT template is configured.
  5. The source fields required by the rules are present.
  6. The appropriate migration scope is selected.
  7. The generated output is validated.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If Auto-Detect cannot identify the source, verify:

  • The source file contains column headers.
  • The headers correspond to fields defined in the MCO.
  • The MCO has been imported/configured.
  • Source-field prefixes exist in the MCO specification.
  • The migration object has a valid configuration.
  • The source file is actually associated with a configured migration.

If the wrong migration object is detected, compare the source headers against the signatures of the possible MCO objects.

docs.title: Standard vs Auto-Detect
docs.text:
The main difference is how the migration configuration is identified.

STANDARD MIGRATION

User selects configuration
        │
        ▼
Migration

AUTO-DETECT MIGRATION

Source File
    │
    ▼
Analyze Headers
    │
    ▼
Identify Configuration
    │
    ▼
Migration

After the configuration has been identified, the same core migration concepts still apply:

Source
  +
Configuration
  +
Rules
  +
SDT Template
  │
  ▼
M3 Output

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
Use Auto-Detect to assist with identifying unknown source files, but always verify the detected migration configuration before using the resulting file for an M3 load.

A successful detection means:

The source structure appears to match a known migration object.

It does not automatically mean:

The source data and transformation rules have been fully validated.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text: Continue to Load by ID to learn how a migration can retrieve and process specific records using identifiers instead of processing an entire source dataset.

docs.title: Batch Migration
docs.text:
The Batch Migration function is used to execute multiple migration jobs as part of a single migration process.

Instead of running each migration configuration individually, Batch Migration allows a group of migration jobs to be processed together.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
During a migration cycle, several related M3 objects may need to be generated.

Running them individually would require:

Migration 1
    ↓
Wait
    ↓
Migration 2
    ↓
Wait
    ↓
Migration 3

Batch Migration provides a more efficient workflow:

Batch
 │
 ├── Migration 1
 ├── Migration 2
 ├── Migration 3
 └── Migration 4
        │
        ▼
 Execute Jobs
        │
        ▼
Generated Migration Files

docs.title: When to Use Batch Migration
docs.text:
Batch Migration is useful when:

  • Multiple migration objects need to be processed.
  • Several configured migrations belong to the same migration cycle.
  • The migration configurations have already been tested individually.
  • Multiple M3 load files need to be regenerated.
  • A repeatable group of migration jobs is required.

docs.title: Before Running a Batch
docs.text:
Each migration included in the batch should already have a valid configuration.

Verify:

Source Map
    ✓

Migration Map
    ✓

Rule Configuration
    ✓

SDT Template
    ✓

Transaction Sheets
    ✓

Batch Migration should normally be used after the individual migrations have been tested successfully.

!!! important Batch processing does not replace migration validation. Each migration configuration should be tested before it becomes part of a larger batch.

docs.title: Batch Migration Flow
docs.text:
The general process is:

Batch Configuration
        │
        ▼
Load Migration Jobs
        │
        ▼
Process Job 1
        │
        ▼
Process Job 2
        │
        ▼
Process Job 3
        │
        ▼
Generate Output Files

Each job uses the same core migration engine as an individual migration.

docs.title: Individual Job Processing
docs.text:
For each migration job, the Data Migration Tool performs the normal migration workflow:

Migration Job
     │
     ▼
Resolve Source
     │
     ▼
Load Source Data
     │
     ▼
Load Rule Configuration
     │
     ▼
Apply FILTER Rules
     │
     ▼
Apply Transformation Rules
     │
     ▼
Resolve SDT Configuration
     │
     ▼
Generate Output

The batch functionality coordinates multiple executions of this process.

docs.title: Example Batch
docs.text:
A migration cycle could contain:

Item Master
Item Facility
Item Warehouse

The batch would conceptually execute:

Batch Migration
│
├── Item Master
│      └── MMS200MI
│
├── Item Facility
│      └── Configured API
│
└── Item Warehouse
       └── Configured API

Each migration can have its own:

  • Source
  • Rule Configuration
  • API
  • SDT Template
  • Transaction sheets

docs.title: Migration Dependencies
docs.text:
The order of migration objects may be important.

For example:

Item Master
     │
     ▼
Item Facility
     │
     ▼
Item Warehouse

If one migration object logically depends on another, the batch should respect the approved migration sequence.

!!! warning Do not assume that migration jobs can always be executed in any order. Follow the migration sequence defined for the M3 implementation.

docs.title: Rule Configurations
docs.text:
Each migration job continues to use its own Rule Configuration.

For example:

Batch
 │
 ├── Migration A
 │      └── Rules A
 │
 ├── Migration B
 │      └── Rules B
 │
 └── Migration C
        └── Rules C

Changes to one Rule Configuration therefore affect the corresponding migration when the batch is executed.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Where applicable, the migration scope must also be considered.

For example:

GLOBAL
DIV_US
DIV_CA

Scope-specific rules may produce different results from the same source data.

Before running a production batch, verify that the appropriate scope is being used for the migration jobs.

docs.title: Output Files
docs.text:
Each migration job generates its corresponding M3 load output.

Conceptually:

Batch Run
 │
 ├── Item Master
 │      └── LOAD_....xlsx
 │
 ├── Item Facility
 │      └── LOAD_....xlsx
 │
 └── Item Warehouse
        └── LOAD_....xlsx

Generated files are stored in the configured output location, normally:

output/

docs.title: Monitoring the Batch
docs.text:
During execution, monitor the System Log.

The log provides information about:

  • Migration jobs being processed
  • Source loading
  • Rule processing
  • Generated files
  • Warnings
  • Errors

A batch containing several jobs may take longer than an individual migration.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
If a migration job encounters an error, review the System Log to determine:

Which migration failed?
        │
        ▼
At what stage?
        │
        ├── Source
        ├── Configuration
        ├── Rules
        ├── SDT
        └── Output

Do not assume that all generated files are valid simply because the batch process started successfully.

docs.title: Recommended Batch Workflow
docs.text:
Before a production batch:

  1. Verify the Source Map.
  2. Verify the Migration Map.
  3. Review recent Rule Configuration changes.
  4. Test modified migrations individually.
  5. Confirm the migration sequence.
  6. Confirm the appropriate scope.
  7. Run the batch.
  8. Review the System Log.
  9. Verify all expected output files were generated.
  10. Validate record counts.
  11. Validate transformed values.
  12. Confirm the files are ready for the next migration stage.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Batch validation should occur at two levels.

docs.title: Batch-Level Validation
docs.text:
Confirm that every expected migration was processed.

For example:

Expected Jobs: 5
Generated Files: 5

Investigate any difference.

docs.title: Migration-Level Validation
docs.text:
Each generated file must still be validated individually.

For example:

Item Master
│
├── Record count
├── Required fields
├── Rule results
└── SDT structure

Item Facility
│
├── Record count
├── Required fields
├── Rule results
└── SDT structure

A successful batch execution does not automatically mean that the business transformation results are correct.

docs.title: Batch vs Standard Migration
docs.text:
Standard Migration processes one migration configuration:

Configuration
      │
      ▼
Migration
      │
      ▼
Output

Batch Migration coordinates multiple migration jobs:

Batch
 │
 ├── Configuration A → Output A
 ├── Configuration B → Output B
 └── Configuration C → Output C

The underlying transformation concepts remain the same.

docs.title: When Not to Use Batch Migration
docs.text:
Avoid using Batch Migration as the first test of a new migration configuration.

Instead:

Develop Rules
     │
     ▼
Load by ID
     │
     ▼
Standard Migration
     │
     ▼
Validate Output
     │
     ▼
Batch Migration

This makes troubleshooting significantly easier.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If a batch migration fails, determine which job caused the problem.

Then test that migration individually using Standard Migration.

Verify:
