  • Source availability
  • Source Map
  • Migration Map
  • Rule Configuration
  • Rule Scope
  • SDT template
  • Transaction sheets
  • Output permissions

For rule-specific problems, use Load by ID to isolate representative records.

docs.title: Recommended Migration Progression
docs.text:
A useful progression for developing a migration is:

Configure Migration
       │
       ▼
Develop Rules
       │
       ▼
Load by ID
       │
       ▼
Standard Migration
       │
       ▼
Validate
       │
       ▼
Batch Migration

This keeps Batch Migration focused on executing configurations that have already been tested and approved.

docs.title: Load by ID
docs.text:
The Load by ID migration mode is used when only specific records need to be migrated instead of processing the entire source dataset.

This is useful for testing, troubleshooting, validation, and targeted migrations.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A Standard Migration typically processes the complete configured source:

Complete Source Dataset
        │
        ▼
Transformation
        │
        ▼
M3 Output

Load by ID adds a record-selection step:

Complete Source Dataset
        │
        ▼
Select Specific ID(s)
        │
        ▼
Matching Records
        │
        ▼
Transformation
        │
        ▼
M3 Output

This allows a smaller population to be processed without changing the original source.

docs.title: When to Use Load by ID
docs.text:
Load by ID is particularly useful for:

  • Testing transformation rules
  • Troubleshooting a specific record
  • Validating a new rule
  • Comparing expected and actual values
  • Reprocessing selected records
  • Creating a small migration sample
  • Investigating source-data issues

For example, instead of migrating thousands of Item Master records, you may want to test:

AP32508
AP32508-2P
RS90001

docs.title: Accessing Load by ID
docs.text:
Navigate to:

Run Migration → Load by ID

The Load by ID screen allows the user to configure a targeted migration.

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
A Load by ID migration follows this general process:

Select Migration Configuration
        │
        ▼
Select Source
        │
        ▼
Define Record ID(s)
        │
        ▼
Retrieve Matching Records
        │
        ▼
Apply FILTER Rules
        │
        ▼
Apply Transformation Rules
        │
        ▼
Generate SDT Output

The transformation process itself remains based on the same Rule Configuration used by the other migration modes.

docs.title: Record Identification
docs.text:
The ID represents the source value used to locate the record or records that should be processed.

For Item Master, for example, the identifier may be:

ITNO

or the corresponding legacy field:

MBITNO

Example source:

MBITNO MBITTY MBPUIT AP32508 FG 1 AP32508-2P FG 3 TEST001 RM 2

If the requested ID is:

AP32508

the targeted dataset becomes:

MBITNO MBITTY MBPUIT AP32508 FG 1

Only the selected record continues through the migration process.

docs.title: Multiple IDs
docs.text:
Load by ID can be useful when a small group of related records needs to be tested.

For example:

AP32508
AP32508-2P
AP32508-3P

Conceptually:

Requested IDs
     │
     ├── AP32508
     ├── AP32508-2P
     └── AP32508-3P
     │
     ▼
Source Lookup
     │
     ▼
Matching Records
     │
     ▼
Migration

This provides a controlled test population.

docs.title: Rule Processing
docs.text:
After the requested records are retrieved, the normal transformation rules are applied.

For example, consider:

MBITNO = AP32508
MMITTY = FG
MBPUIT = 1

A PLCD Python rule may evaluate:

itno = str(
    row.get("ITNO", row.get("MBITNO", ""))
).strip().upper()

itty = str(
    row.get("ITTY", row.get("MMITTY", ""))
).strip().upper()

puit = str(
    row.get("PUIT", row.get("MBPUIT", ""))
).strip()

if itno.startswith(("RS9", "ZZ")):
    return "00"

if itty in ("RM", "PK") and puit == "2":
    return "01"

if itty in ("SF", "FG") and puit == "1":
    return "02"

if puit == "3":
    return "05"

return ""

For:

ITNO = AP32508
ITTY = FG
PUIT = 1

the expected result is:

PLCD = 02

This makes Load by ID particularly useful when validating complex rules.

docs.title: Troubleshooting with Load by ID
docs.text:
Load by ID can help isolate transformation problems.

Instead of reviewing:

50,000 source records

you can isolate:

1 source record

and compare:

Raw Source
    │
    ▼
Rule Dependencies
    │
    ▼
Business Requirement
    │
    ▼
Expected Result
    │
    ▼
Actual Output

docs.title: Example Troubleshooting Process
docs.text:
Suppose:

ITNO = AP32508

produces an unexpected PLCD.

First review the complete source record:

MBITNO = AP32508
MMITTY = FG
MBPUIT = 1

Then identify the rule dependencies:

PLCD
 │
 ├── ITNO
 ├── ITTY
 └── PUIT

Determine the expected result:

ITTY = FG
PUIT = 1

Expected:

PLCD = 02

Run only:

AP32508

using Load by ID and compare the generated value.

This makes it easier to determine whether the problem comes from:

  • Source data
  • Source-field naming
  • Rule logic
  • Rule scope
  • Condition priority
  • Migration configuration

docs.title: Load by ID and Scope
docs.text:
The selected migration scope still matters.

For example:

Record:
AP32508

GLOBAL
    ↓
PLCD = 02

DIV_US
    ↓
PLCD = 03

The same record may produce different results when a scope-specific override exists.

Always verify the selected scope when using Load by ID for rule testing.

docs.title: Load by ID vs FILTER
docs.text:
Load by ID and FILTER rules both reduce the migration population, but they serve different purposes.

Load by ID FILTER User selects specific records Business logic selects records Usually temporary Stored in Rule Configuration Useful for testing Used during normal migration Targets known IDs Evaluates conditions

For example:

Load by ID:

Process AP32508 only

versus:

FILTER:

Process every record where MBSTAT = 20

docs.title: Load by ID vs Standard Migration
docs.text:
STANDARD

Configured Source
      │
      ▼
All Applicable Records
      │
      ▼
Migration

LOAD BY ID

Configured Source
      │
      ▼
Requested IDs
      │
      ▼
Matching Records
      │
      ▼
Migration

The main difference is the population being processed.

The transformation rules and M3 output requirements remain the same.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
After running Load by ID, compare the generated output with the original source record.

For each tested field:

Source Value
     +
Business Requirement
     +
Transformation Rule
     │
     ▼
Expected M3 Value
     ↕
Actual M3 Value

This is especially useful when developing new PYTHON rules.

docs.title: Recommended Testing Workflow
docs.text:
When developing or changing a transformation rule:

  1. Identify representative source records.
  2. Include normal cases.
  3. Include special cases.
  4. Include blank/null cases when applicable.
  5. Determine the expected result for each record.
  6. Run the selected records using Load by ID.
  7. Compare the generated output.
  8. Correct the rule if necessary.
  9. Repeat the test.
  10. Run a larger migration only after the targeted tests pass.

For example:

Test Record Scenario Expected AP32508 FG / PUIT 1 PLCD 02 TEST001 PK / PUIT 2 PLCD 01 RS90001 RS9 Item PLCD 00 TEST003 PUIT 3 PLCD 05

docs.title: Important Consideration
docs.text:
A successful Load by ID run proves that the selected records were processed successfully.

It does not prove that every possible source-data scenario has been tested.

Use representative records covering all important business-rule conditions before approving a transformation.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If a requested record is not found, verify:

  • The correct source is selected.
  • The correct identifier field is being used.
  • The ID exists in the source.
  • Leading or trailing spaces are not affecting the comparison.
  • The source value has the expected format.
  • The database/source connection is available.
  • The correct migration configuration is selected.

If the record is found but produces incorrect output, review:

  • Rule dependencies
  • Source values
  • Rule type
  • Python condition order
  • Selected scope
  • Expected business requirement

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text: Continue to Batch Migration to learn how multiple migration configurations can be processed as part of a larger migration run.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Documentation coming soon.

docs.title: Standard Migration
docs.text:
The Standard Migration is the primary method for running a configured migration in the Data Migration Tool.

It allows the user to select a Rule Configuration, choose the corresponding legacy source, optionally select a business-unit scope, and generate the M3 SDT output.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Standard Migration should be used when the migration object has already been configured and the source data is known.

The basic process is:

Rule Configuration
        +
Legacy Source
        +
Migration Scope
        │
        ▼
Data Migration Tool
        │
        ▼
Apply FILTER Rules
        │
        ▼
Apply Transformation Rules
        │
        ▼
Populate SDT Template
        │
        ▼
M3 Migration Output

docs.title: Accessing Standard Migration
docs.text:
Navigate to:

Run Migration → Standard Migration

The Standard Migration screen provides the options required to execute the migration.

docs.title: 1. Select Rule Configuration
docs.text:
Select the Rule Configuration associated with the migration.

For example:

MMS200MI

The Rule Configuration determines how legacy source fields are transformed into M3 target fields.

It contains information such as:

TARGET_FIELD
SOURCE_FIELD
RULE_TYPE
RULE_VALUE
SCOPE

Example:

MBITNO
   │
   │ DIRECT
   ▼
ITNO

For more complex transformations:

ITNO ──┐
ITTY ──┼──► PYTHON Rule ──► PLCD
PUIT ──┘

docs.title: 2. Select Source Data
docs.text:
Select the migration business object containing the source data.

For example:

Item Master
Item Facility
Item Warehouse
Supplier
Customer

The available selections come from:

config/source_map.csv

The selected business object is then resolved to its configured source.

Example:

Item Master
     │
     ▼
Source Map
     │
     ▼
raw_data/ItemMaster.xlsx

The source may be:

Excel
CSV
SQL

docs.title: 3. Select Scope
docs.text:
The Scope option determines which version of the transformation rules should be applied.

The default is:

GLOBAL

Additional business-unit scopes may also be available.

For example:

GLOBAL
DIV_US
DIV_CA

If no business-specific transformation is required, use:

GLOBAL

docs.title: GLOBAL and Scope Overrides
docs.text:
GLOBAL rules provide the default transformation behavior.

For example:

PLCD / GLOBAL

A business unit may override that rule:

PLCD / DIV_US

When:

Scope = DIV_US

the business-specific PLCD rule is used instead of the GLOBAL PLCD rule.

Other fields continue using their GLOBAL rules unless they also have an override.

docs.title: 4. Run Migration
docs.text:
After selecting:

Rule Configuration
Source Data
Scope

click:

RUN MIGRATION

The application begins processing the migration.

docs.title: What Happens During Standard Migration?
docs.text:
The application performs several steps automatically.

START
  │
  ▼
Resolve Source
  │
  ▼
Load Legacy Data
  │
  ▼
Load Rule Configuration
  │
  ▼
Apply FILTER Rules
  │
  ▼
Transform Target Fields
  │
  ▼
Resolve Migration Map
  │
  ├── API
  ├── SDT Template
  └── Transaction Sheets
  │
  ▼
Populate SDT
  │
  ▼
Save Output

docs.title: Loading the Source
docs.text:
The Data Extractor loads the configured source.

For an Excel source:

Excel File
    │
    ▼
DataFrame

For CSV:

CSV File
    │
    ▼
DataFrame

For SQL:

SQL Query
    │
    ▼
SQL Server
    │
    ▼
DataFrame

Once loaded, the source columns become available to the transformation rules.

docs.title: FILTER Processing
docs.text:
FILTER rules are processed before the target transformations.

For example:

Source
10,000 records
     │
     ▼
FILTER Rules
     │
     ▼
8,450 records

Only the remaining records continue through the migration.

If every record is filtered out, the migration cannot continue.

docs.title: Transformation Processing
docs.text:
The Rule Configuration determines how each M3 target field is populated.

For example:

docs.title: DIRECT
docs.text:
MBITNO
   │
   ▼
ITNO

docs.title: CONST
docs.text:
100
 │
 ▼
CONO

docs.title: MAP
docs.text:
Legacy Code
    │
    ▼
Mapping
    │
    ▼
M3 Code

docs.title: PYTHON
docs.text:
Multiple Source Fields
         │
         ▼
    Business Logic
         │
         ▼
     Target Value

docs.title: Migration Map Resolution
docs.text:
The selected MCO business object is used to resolve the corresponding Migration Map configuration.

The Migration Map identifies:

API_NAME
SDT_TEMPLATE
TRANSACTION_SHEET

Conceptually:

MCO Business Object
        │
        ▼
Migration Map
        │
        ├── API
        ├── SDT
        └── Transaction Sheets

docs.title: SDT Generation
docs.text:
After transformation, the resulting values are written into the configured M3 SDT template.

Transformed Data
       │
       ▼
SDT Template
       │
       ▼
Transaction Sheet(s)
       │
       ▼
Generated Workbook

The original SDT structure is used as the foundation for the generated migration file.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
The generated migration file is normally saved under:

output/

The System Log provides information about the migration process and generated output.

docs.title: Monitor the System Log
docs.text:
While the migration runs, review the System Log.

The log can provide information about:

Source loading
Rule loading
FILTER processing
Transformation
SDT generation
Warnings
Errors
Output location

If the migration fails, the System Log should be one of the first places reviewed.

docs.title: Example Standard Migration
docs.text:
Suppose you want to migrate Item Master.

Select:

Rule Configuration:
MMS200MI

Source:
Item Master

Scope:
GLOBAL

The application resolves:

Item Master
    │
    ├── Source Map
    │      └── Legacy Item Source
    │
    └── Migration Map
           ├── MMS200MI
           ├── SDT Template
           └── Transaction Sheets

The rules are then applied and the M3 migration workbook is generated.

docs.title: Before Running the Migration
docs.text:
Verify:

  • [ ] Correct Rule Configuration
  • [ ] Correct source
  • [ ] Correct scope
  • [ ] Source data is available
  • [ ] Rule changes have been saved
  • [ ] Required mapping files exist
  • [ ] SDT template exists
  • [ ] Migration Map is configured

docs.title: After Running the Migration
docs.text:
Do not stop validation at:

Migration Completed Successfully

Review the generated output.

Validate:

  • [ ] Expected record count
  • [ ] Required target fields
  • [ ] DIRECT transformations
  • [ ] MAP transformations
  • [ ] Important PYTHON rules
  • [ ] Scope-specific rules
  • [ ] SDT transaction sheets
  • [ ] Representative business records

docs.title: Successful Execution vs Successful Migration
docs.text:
These are not necessarily the same thing.

Successful Execution

The application completed
without a technical failure.

versus:

Successful Migration

The application completed
        +
The resulting data matches
the approved business requirements.

A migration should only be considered ready after the generated output has been validated.

docs.title: When to Use Another Migration Mode
docs.text:
Use Auto-Detect Migration when:

You have a source file but are unsure which migration configuration should process it.

Use Load by ID when:

You want to test or migrate specific records.

Use Batch Migration when:

Multiple already-configured migrations need to be processed together.

Use Standard Migration when:

You know the migration configuration and want to process its configured source normally.

docs.title: Recommended Workflow
docs.text:
For a new or modified migration:

Configure
    │
    ▼
Develop Rules
    │
    ▼
Load by ID
    │
    ▼
Validate Test Cases
    │
    ▼
Standard Migration
    │
    ▼
Validate Complete Output
    │
    ▼
Batch Migration

This progression makes rule problems easier to identify before processing larger migration populations.

docs.title: FILTER Rules
docs.text:
A FILTER rule determines which source records are allowed to continue through the migration process.

Unlike other rule types, a FILTER rule does not calculate an M3 target value.

Instead, it determines whether a source row should be included or excluded.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
A source file may contain records that should not be migrated.

For example:

Legacy Source
│
├── Active Item
├── Active Item
├── Obsolete Item
├── Test Item
└── Active Item

A FILTER rule can remove records that do not meet the migration criteria.

The result becomes:

Migration Dataset
│
├── Active Item
├── Active Item
└── Active Item

docs.title: When FILTER Rules Are Applied
docs.text:
FILTER rules are applied before target field transformations.

The migration flow is:

Legacy Source Data
        │
        ▼
     FILTER
        │
        ▼
Remaining Records
        │
        ▼
Transformation Rules
        │
        ▼
M3 SDT Output

This means that records excluded by a FILTER rule are not processed by the remaining transformation rules.

docs.title: Basic FILTER Structure
docs.text:
A FILTER rule typically contains:

RULE_TYPE    = FILTER
SOURCE_FIELD = <source column>
RULE_VALUE   = <condition>

The condition determines whether a row should remain in the migration dataset.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
Assume only active records should be migrated.

Source:

MBSTAT

Possible values:

20
90

Business requirement:

Keep rows where MBSTAT = 20

FILTER rule:

source == "20"

If:

MBSTAT = 20

the row is kept.

If:

MBSTAT = 90

the row is excluded.

docs.title: Using the Full Row
docs.text:
A FILTER rule can also evaluate other source fields through row.

Example:

str(row.get("MMITTY", "")).strip().upper() != "ZZ"

This keeps rows where:

MMITTY <> ZZ

docs.title: Multiple Conditions
docs.text:
Filters can evaluate multiple conditions.

Example:

status = str(row.get("MBSTAT", "")).strip()
itty = str(row.get("MMITTY", "")).strip().upper()

status == "20" and itty != "ZZ"

This means:

Keep the row when:

MBSTAT = 20

AND

MMITTY <> ZZ

docs.title: Keep Logic vs Exclude Logic
docs.text:
FILTER conditions represent rows that should be kept.

For example:

source == "20"

means:

Keep rows where the source value equals 20.

It does not mean:

Delete rows where the source equals 20.

This distinction is important when writing filter logic.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Source data:

ITNO STAT A100 20 A200 90 A300 20 A400 90

FILTER:

source == "20"

Result:

ITNO STAT A100 20 A300 20

Only the records matching the condition continue into the transformation process.

docs.title: Multiple FILTER Rules
docs.text:
If multiple FILTER rules exist, each filter is applied to the remaining dataset.

Conceptually:

Original Dataset
      │
      ▼
Filter 1
      │
      ▼
Remaining Rows
      │
      ▼
Filter 2
      │
      ▼
Final Migration Dataset

Therefore, filters should be reviewed carefully because each additional filter can reduce the number of migrated records.

docs.title: Migration Stops When Everything Is Filtered
docs.text:
If FILTER rules remove every record, the migration is aborted.

The System Log may report that all rows were filtered out.

This protects the tool from generating an empty migration file unintentionally.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
Before creating a FILTER rule:

  1. Define the business population that should be migrated.
  2. Identify the source fields required to determine eligibility.
  3. Write the condition as a keep condition.
  4. Test the filter against known records.
  5. Compare the row count before and after filtering.
  6. Review excluded records before production migration.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Suppose the source contains:

10,000 records

After filtering:

8,450 records

The migration team should understand why:

1,550 records

were excluded.

A successful migration should not only generate a file. The resulting record population should also match the approved migration scope.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If too many records are excluded, verify:

  • The correct source field is being used.
  • String and numeric comparisons are correct.
  • Blank values are handled correctly.
  • Multiple filters are not unintentionally removing the same population.
  • The condition represents rows to keep, not rows to delete.

For example:

source != "90"

keeps everything except 90.

While:

source == "90"

keeps only 90.

These two filters produce completely different migration populations.

docs.title: MAP Rules
docs.text:
A MAP rule is used when a source value must be translated into a different target value using a lookup table.

This is useful when legacy codes do not match the values expected by M3.

docs.title: When to Use a MAP Rule
docs.text:
Use a MAP rule when:

  • The source value must be converted into another code
  • There are many value-to-value translations
  • The mapping is easier to maintain in a table than in Python logic
  • Business users may need to review or update the mapping

Example:

Legacy Value    M3 Value
------------    --------
A               01
B               02
C               03

If the legacy source contains:

A

the MAP rule returns:

01

docs.title: Basic MAP Structure
docs.text:
A typical MAP rule contains:

TARGET_FIELD = <M3 field>
SOURCE_FIELD = <legacy source field>
RULE_TYPE    = MAP
RULE_VALUE   = <mapping configuration>

The SOURCE_FIELD provides the value that must be translated.

The RULE_VALUE identifies the lookup definition used by the transformation engine.

docs.title: External Mapping Files
docs.text:
The Data Migration Tool can load mapping values from an external Excel or CSV file.

The mapping configuration uses this format:

path|key_column|value_column

Example:

config/maps/item_status.xlsx|LEGACY_STATUS|M3_STATUS

This means:

File:
config/maps/item_status.xlsx

Lookup key:
LEGACY_STATUS

Returned value:
M3_STATUS

docs.title: Example Mapping File
docs.text:
Example Excel file:

LEGACY_STATUS M3_STATUS A 10 B 20 C 30

Rule:

TARGET_FIELD = STAT
SOURCE_FIELD = MBSTAT
RULE_TYPE    = MAP
RULE_VALUE   = config/maps/item_status.xlsx|LEGACY_STATUS|M3_STATUS

Source:

MBSTAT = B

Result:

STAT = 20

docs.title: How MAP Processing Works
docs.text:
The transformation flow is:

SOURCE_FIELD
     │
     ▼
Normalize Source Value
     │
     ▼
Mapping Table
     │
     ▼
TARGET Value

The tool normalizes the source lookup value before matching.

For example:

" a "

is treated as:

"A"

This helps reduce problems caused by spaces or capitalization differences.

docs.title: Duplicate Mapping Keys
docs.text:
The mapping file should contain one target value per source key.

Avoid configurations like:

SOURCE_KEY    TARGET_VALUE
----------    ------------
A             01
A             02

A duplicate key creates ambiguity.

The mapping file should instead contain:

A → 01

or:

A → 02

depending on the approved business requirement.

docs.title: Missing Mapping Values
docs.text:
If the source value does not exist in the lookup table, the result may be blank.

For example:

Source:

MBSTAT = X

Mapping:

A → 10
B → 20
C → 30

There is no mapping for:

X

Therefore the target value cannot be resolved.

!!! warning Before using a MAP rule in production migration, verify that all expected source values exist in the mapping table.

docs.title: When MAP is Better Than PYTHON
docs.text:
Consider this requirement:

A → 10
B → 20
C → 30
D → 40
E → 50
F → 60

This could be written in Python:

if source == "A":
    return "10"
if source == "B":
    return "20"
if source == "C":
    return "30"

However, this becomes difficult to maintain when many values are involved.

A MAP rule is preferable because the values can be managed in a table.

Use:

MAP

for lookup-style transformations.

Use:

PYTHON

when the target depends on conditions or multiple fields.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
When creating a MAP rule:

  1. Identify the source field.
  2. List all known source values.
  3. Define the corresponding M3 values.
  4. Store the mapping in a controlled Excel or CSV file.
  5. Configure the MAP rule.
  6. Test every expected source value.
  7. Review unmapped values before migration.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If a MAP rule returns blank or incorrect values, verify:

  • The mapping file exists.
  • The file path is correct.
  • The key column exists.
  • The value column exists.
  • The source field contains the expected values.
  • The mapping table does not contain unexpected duplicates.
  • The source value exists in the mapping table.

docs.title: Example Validation
docs.text:
Source data:

MBSTAT A B C

Expected M3 output:

STAT 10 20 30

The generated migration output should be compared against this expected mapping before the file is accepted.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Documentation coming soon.

docs.title: Python Rules
docs.text:
A PYTHON rule is used when a target field requires transformation logic that cannot be handled by a simple DIRECT, CONST, or MAP rule.

Python rules allow the Data Migration Tool to evaluate values from the complete source row and apply custom business logic before generating the M3 target value.

docs.title: When to Use a Python Rule
docs.text:
Use a Python rule when the target value depends on:

  • Multiple source fields
  • Conditional logic
  • Multiple business conditions
  • String manipulation
  • Numeric calculations
  • Blank or null handling
  • A combination of the above

For example:

ITNO ──┐
       │
ITTY ──┼──► Python Rule ──► PLCD
       │
PUIT ──┘

In this case, PLCD cannot be determined from only one source field.

docs.title: Basic Structure
docs.text:
A Python rule normally reads values, evaluates the business conditions, and returns the resulting target value.

Example:

puit = str(row.get("PUIT", row.get("MBPUIT", ""))).strip()

if puit == "1":
    return "00"

if puit == "2":
    return "11"

if puit == "3":
    return "12"

return ""

The final return determines the value written to the target field.

docs.title: source
docs.text:
source represents the value obtained from the field defined in SOURCE_FIELD.

Example:

if source is None:
    return ""

return str(source).strip()

For simple transformations, using source may be sufficient.

docs.title: row
docs.text:
row provides access to the complete source record.

For example:

itno = row.get("MBITNO", "")
puit = row.get("MBPUIT", "")

This makes it possible for one target rule to depend on multiple source columns.

Example:

itty = str(row.get("MMITTY", "")).strip().upper()
puit = str(row.get("MBPUIT", "")).strip()

if itty == "FG" and puit == "1":
    return "02"

return ""

docs.title: Handling Alternative Column Names
docs.text:
Source files may not always use the same column naming convention.

For example, a field could appear as:

PUIT

or:

MBPUIT

A Python rule can support both:

puit = str(
    row.get("PUIT", row.get("MBPUIT", ""))
).strip()

The rule first searches for PUIT.

If it does not exist, it searches for MBPUIT.

If neither exists, it returns an empty string.

This pattern can also be used for other fields:

itno = str(
    row.get("ITNO", row.get("MBITNO", ""))
).strip().upper()

itty = str(
    row.get("ITTY", row.get("MMITTY", ""))
).strip().upper()

docs.title: Normalize Values Before Comparing
docs.text:
Values should normally be cleaned before conditions are evaluated.

For text fields:

value = str(row.get("FIELD", "")).strip().upper()

This performs three operations:

Convert to string
       ↓
Remove spaces
       ↓
Convert to uppercase

For example:

" fg "

becomes:

"FG"

This helps prevent conditions from failing because of capitalization or unwanted spaces.

docs.title: Example: PLCD
docs.text:
Consider the following business requirement:

If ITNO starts with RS9 or ZZ
    → 00

If ITTY is RM or PK and PUIT = 2
    → 01

If ITTY is SF or FG and PUIT = 1
    → 02

If PUIT = 3
    → 05

The Python rule can be written as:

itno = str(
    row.get("ITNO", row.get("MBITNO", ""))
).strip().upper()

itty = str(
    row.get("ITTY", row.get("MMITTY", ""))
).strip().upper()

puit = str(
    row.get("PUIT", row.get("MBPUIT", ""))
).strip()

if itno.startswith(("RS9", "ZZ")):
    return "00"

if itty in ("RM", "PK") and puit == "2":
    return "01"

if itty in ("SF", "FG") and puit == "1":
    return "02"

if puit == "3":
    return "05"

return ""

docs.title: Condition Order Matters
docs.text:
Python rules are evaluated from top to bottom.

Consider:

if puit == "3":
    return "05"

if itty == "FG" and puit == "3":
    return "02"

If:

ITTY = FG
PUIT = 3

the result will be:

05

The second condition will never be evaluated because the first condition already returned a value.

Therefore, condition priority must match the business requirement.

!!! warning When multiple conditions can match the same record, place the highest-priority condition first.

docs.title: Blank Values
docs.text:
Python rules should explicitly consider blank values when necessary.

Example:

value = str(source).strip() if source is not None else ""

if value == "":
    return ""

This prevents blank values from accidentally being interpreted as meaningful data.

docs.title: Returning the Original Source Value
docs.text:
Sometimes a transformation should apply only under certain conditions and otherwise preserve the source value.

Example:

value = str(source).strip() if source is not None else ""

if value == "PQ":
    return "QC"

return value

This means:

PQ → QC
ON → ON
MB → MB

docs.title: Returning a Constant from a Condition
docs.text:
Python rules can also return constants based on another field.

Example requirement:

If PUIT = 1 → NOR
If PUIT = 2 → INV
If PUIT = 3 → D22

Rule:

puit = str(
    row.get("PUIT", row.get("MBPUIT", ""))
).strip()

if puit == "1":
    return "NOR"

if puit == "2":
    return "INV"

if puit == "3":
    return "D22"

return ""

docs.title: Multiple Conditions
docs.text:
Conditions can be combined using and.

Example:

itty = str(row.get("MMITTY", "")).strip().upper()
eoqm = str(row.get("MBEOQM", "")).strip()

if itty == "FG" and eoqm == "12":
    return "010"

return "020"

This represents:

ITTY = FG
   AND
EOQM = 12
    │
    ▼
   010

Otherwise
    │
    ▼
   020

docs.title: Testing a Python Rule
docs.text:
A Python rule should always be tested using known source records.

For example:

ITNO ITTY PUIT Expected PLCD RS90001 RM 2 00 AP32508 FG 1 02 TEST01 PK 2 01 TEST02 FG 3 05

After running the migration, compare the generated output against the expected results.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: When a Python rule produces an unexpected value, verify the following:

docs.title: 1. Source column name
docs.text:
Confirm that the rule is reading the correct source column.

For example:

MMITTY

is different from:

MBITTY

A rule referencing the wrong column may return a blank value without producing an obvious error.

docs.title: 2. Actual source value
docs.text:
Check the raw source record.

Do not assume the value in the generated output represents what existed in the source.

docs.title: 3. Data type
docs.text:
Values loaded from Excel may be represented differently than expected.

For migration codes, converting values to strings before comparison is generally recommended.

puit = str(row.get("MBPUIT", "")).strip()

Then compare:

if puit == "3":

rather than:

if puit == 3:

docs.title: 4. Condition order
docs.text: Verify that an earlier condition is not returning a value before the intended condition is reached.

docs.title: 5. Dependencies
docs.text:
Identify every source field required by the rule.

For example:

PLCD
 │
 ├── ITNO
 ├── ITTY
 └── PUIT

When troubleshooting PLCD, all three source values should be reviewed.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
Keep Python rules focused on the business requirement.

Prefer:

puit = str(row.get("MBPUIT", "")).strip()

if puit == "1":
    return "00"

if puit == "2":
    return "11"

if puit == "3":
    return "12"

return ""

over unnecessarily complex logic.

A rule should be understandable by another migration team member who needs to maintain it later.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
See:

  • Understanding the Rule Configuration
  • MAP Rules
  • FILTER Rules
  • Rule Troubleshooting

docs.title: Understanding the Rule Configuration
docs.text:
The Rule Configuration defines how legacy source data is transformed into the values required by the target M3 SDT.

It is one of the core components of the Data Migration Tool.

A migration may have a valid source file and the correct SDT template, but without the appropriate transformation rules, the target fields cannot be populated correctly.

docs.title: Role of Rules in a Migration
docs.text:
The migration process can be represented as:

Legacy Source Data
        │
        ▼
┌──────────────────────┐
│  Rule Configuration  │
│                      │
│  TARGET_FIELD        │
│  SOURCE_FIELD        │
│  RULE_TYPE           │
│  RULE_VALUE          │
│  SCOPE               │
└──────────┬───────────┘
           │
           ▼
 Transformation Engine
           │
           ▼
      M3 SDT Output

The Rule Configuration tells the Transformation Engine:

  • Which M3 field must be populated
  • Where the source value comes from
  • How the value must be transformed
  • Whether special business logic is required
  • Whether the rule applies globally or to a specific scope

docs.title: Rule Configuration Files
docs.text:
Rule Configuration files are stored in:

config/rules/

Each M3 program or migration configuration can have its own rule file.

For example:

config/rules/MMS200MI.xlsx

A Rule Configuration contains a Rules worksheet where the transformation logic is defined.

docs.title: Rule Structure
docs.text:
Each row in the Rules worksheet represents the transformation logic for a target field.

The main columns are:

Column Purpose TARGET_FIELD M3 destination field SOURCE_FIELD Field containing the legacy/source value RULE_TYPE Transformation method RULE_VALUE Additional logic or configuration SCOPE Determines where the rule applies

docs.title: TARGET_FIELD
docs.text:
TARGET_FIELD identifies the field that will be populated in the M3 SDT.

For example:

PLCD

The target field must correspond to a field available in the applicable SDT transaction sheet.

A simplified rule could therefore look like:

TARGET_FIELD = PLCD

Meaning:

This rule determines the value that will be written to the M3 field PLCD.

docs.title: SOURCE_FIELD
docs.text:
SOURCE_FIELD identifies the legacy field used as the primary source for the transformation.

Example:

SOURCE_FIELD = MBPUIT

For a simple direct transformation:

MBPUIT
   │
   ▼
Transformation Rule
   │
   ▼
PUIT

However, some rules require more than one source field.

For example, a PLCD rule may need information from:

ITNO
ITTY
PUIT

In these situations, a Python rule can access additional values from the complete source row.

docs.title: RULE_TYPE
docs.text:
RULE_TYPE determines how the source value will be transformed.

The Data Migration Tool supports different transformation methods.

Common rule types include:

Rule Type Purpose DIRECT Copy a source value directly CONST Assign a fixed value MAP Translate a source value using a lookup PYTHON Execute custom transformation logic FILTER Determine which source records should be processed

Each rule type is documented separately.

docs.title: DIRECT Rules
docs.text:
A DIRECT rule copies the value from the source field to the target field.

Example:

TARGET_FIELD = ITNO
SOURCE_FIELD = MBITNO
RULE_TYPE    = DIRECT

Result:

MBITNO = AP32508

        ↓

ITNO = AP32508

Use DIRECT when no transformation is required.

docs.title: CONST Rules
docs.text:
A CONST rule assigns the same value to the target field for every applicable record.

Example:

TARGET_FIELD = CONO
RULE_TYPE    = CONST
RULE_VALUE   = 100

Result:

CONO = 100

The source record does not need to contain the value.

docs.title: MAP Rules
docs.text:
A MAP rule converts a source value into another value using a predefined mapping.

Conceptually:

Source Value
     │
     ▼
 Lookup Mapping
     │
     ▼
Target Value

For example:

Legacy Value    M3 Value
------------    --------
A               01
B               02
C               03

If the source contains:

A

the resulting target value becomes:

01

docs.title: PYTHON Rules
docs.text:
PYTHON rules are used when the transformation requires business logic that cannot be represented by a simple direct mapping, constant, or lookup.

For example:

itno = str(row.get("ITNO", row.get("MBITNO", ""))).strip().upper()
itty = str(row.get("ITTY", row.get("MMITTY", ""))).strip().upper()
puit = str(row.get("PUIT", row.get("MBPUIT", ""))).strip()

if itno.startswith(("RS9", "ZZ")):
    return "00"

if itty in ("RM", "PK") and puit == "2":
    return "01"

if itty in ("SF", "FG") and puit == "1":
    return "02"

if puit == "3":
    return "05"

return ""

This type of rule can evaluate multiple fields from the same source row before determining the target value.

Python rules are particularly useful when the transformation contains:

  • Multiple conditions
  • IF/ELSE logic
  • Dependencies on several source columns
  • String manipulation
  • Numeric calculations
  • Business-specific transformation logic

!!! warning Python rules should be tested carefully. An incorrect condition may generate valid-looking output containing incorrect M3 values.

docs.title: FILTER Rules
docs.text:
A FILTER rule controls whether source records should participate in the migration.

Instead of calculating a target value, the rule determines whether a row should be included or excluded.

Conceptually:

Source Records
      │
      ▼
  FILTER Rules
      │
      ├── Keep
      │
      └── Exclude
      │
      ▼
Transformation

Filters are applied before the remaining transformation rules are written to the output.

docs.title: Rule Scope
docs.text:
Rules can also be controlled using SCOPE.

The default scope is:

GLOBAL

A GLOBAL rule represents the default transformation.

Additional scopes can be used when a business unit requires different transformation logic.

For example:

TARGET_FIELD    SCOPE
------------    -------
PLCD            GLOBAL
PLCD            DIV_US

This allows the same target field to have different transformation logic depending on the selected migration scope.

docs.title: Why Rule Order and Dependencies Matter
docs.text:
Some target fields depend on other source values to determine their result.

For example:

             ┌── ITNO
             │
Source Row ──┼── ITTY
             │
             └── PUIT
                  │
                  ▼
              PLCD Rule
                  │
                  ▼
                PLCD

Because of these dependencies, it is important to understand which source columns are required by each rule.

A rule should never assume that another target field has already been calculated unless the transformation process explicitly supports that dependency.

Whenever possible, rules should reference the original source row values.

docs.title: Example: PLCD
docs.text:
Consider the following source record:

MBITNO  = AP32508
MMITTY  = FG
MBPUIT  = 1

A PLCD business rule may state:

If ITNO starts with RS9 or ZZ
    → PLCD = 00

If ITTY is RM or PK and PUIT = 2
    → PLCD = 01

If ITTY is SF or FG and PUIT = 1
    → PLCD = 02

If PUIT = 3
    → PLCD = 05

For this record:

ITTY = FG
PUIT = 1

Therefore:

PLCD = 02

This demonstrates why some target fields cannot simply copy one source column.

docs.title: Recommended Rule Design
docs.text:
When creating a new rule:

  1. Identify the M3 TARGET_FIELD.
  2. Identify the primary SOURCE_FIELD.
  3. Determine whether additional source fields are required.
  4. Select the simplest appropriate RULE_TYPE.
  5. Define the transformation logic.
  6. Determine the appropriate SCOPE.
  7. Test the rule against representative source records.
  8. Validate the generated SDT output.

Whenever possible, prefer simpler rule types.

For example:

DIRECT
   ↓
CONST
   ↓
MAP
   ↓
PYTHON

Use a Python rule when the business requirement actually requires conditional or custom logic.

docs.title: Rule Validation
docs.text:
After creating or modifying a rule, always validate the resulting migration output.

Do not validate only that the migration completed successfully.

A successful execution means that the application was able to process the migration. It does not automatically mean that every transformed value is correct.

Validation should compare:

Source Data
     +
Business Requirement
     +
Rule Configuration
     ↓
Expected M3 Value
     ↕
Actual Generated Value

Any difference between the expected and actual value should be investigated before the generated file is used for migration.

docs.title: Common Errors and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
This section provides guidance for diagnosing common problems when using the Data Migration Tool.

A migration can complete without a technical error while still producing an incorrect business result. Troubleshooting should therefore consider both:

Technical Success
        +
Business Validation
        │
        ▼
Successful Migration

docs.title: Recommended Troubleshooting Approach
docs.text:
When something is wrong, identify where the problem occurs:

Source Data
    │
    ▼
Source Map
    │
    ▼
Migration Map
    │
    ▼
Rule Configuration
    │
    ▼
FILTER Rules
    │
    ▼
Transformation Rules
    │
    ▼
SDT Template
    │
    ▼
Generated Output

Start with the source and work toward the output.

docs.title: Rule Is Not Producing the Expected Value
Symptom
docs.text:
The migration completes, but a target field contains an unexpected value.

Example:

Expected:

PLCD = 02

Actual:

PLCD = 01

docs.title: 1. Verify the raw source record
docs.text:
Do not begin by looking only at the generated output.

Check the actual source values required by the rule.

Example:

MBITNO = AP32508
MMITTY = FG
MBPUIT = 1

docs.title: 2. Identify rule dependencies
docs.text:
For example:

PLCD
 │
 ├── ITNO
 ├── ITTY
 └── PUIT

Verify every dependency.

docs.title: 3. Review the Rule Configuration
docs.text:
Check:

TARGET_FIELD
SOURCE_FIELD
RULE_TYPE
RULE_VALUE
SCOPE

docs.title: 4. Verify the selected scope
docs.text: A scope-specific rule may override the GLOBAL rule.

docs.title: 5. Test the record individually
docs.text: Use Load by ID when possible to isolate the problematic record.

docs.title: Python Rule Returns the Wrong Result
Symptom
docs.text: A PYTHON rule executes successfully but returns an incorrect value.

docs.title: Common Causes
docs.text:
• Wrong source column
  • Incorrect condition order
  • Unexpected spaces
  • Upper/lowercase differences
  • Numeric vs string comparison
  • Missing dependency
  • Blank/null source value

docs.title: Check Column Names
docs.text:
For example:

row.get("MMITTY", "")

is different from:

row.get("MBITTY", "")

A small difference in the field name can completely change the result.

docs.title: Normalize Values
docs.text:
Prefer:

itty = str(row.get("MMITTY", "")).strip().upper()

instead of:

itty = row.get("MMITTY")

For migration codes, converting to strings before comparison is often safer:

puit = str(row.get("MBPUIT", "")).strip()

if puit == "3":
    return "05"

docs.title: Condition Order Problem
docs.text:
Python rules are evaluated from top to bottom.

Example:

if puit == "3":
    return "05"

if itty == "FG" and puit == "3":
    return "02"

For:

ITTY = FG
PUIT = 3

the result is:

05

The second condition is never reached.

When conditions overlap, verify their priority.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: A target field is unexpectedly blank.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Verify that the configured SOURCE_FIELD actually exists in the selected source.

Example:

Rule expects:

MBPUIT

but the source contains:

PUIT

The rule may not receive the expected value.

For Python rules that intentionally support both names:

puit = str(
    row.get("PUIT", row.get("MBPUIT", ""))
).strip()

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: The rule works under GLOBAL but produces a different result for another migration run.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Verify the selected:

Scope

Example:

GLOBAL
PLCD → 02

DIV_US
PLCD → 03

The same source record can produce different results depending on the selected scope.

Also verify the scope defined in the Rule Configuration.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: A rule was modified, but the migration still appears to use previous logic.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
• Confirm the Rule Configuration was saved.
  • Confirm the correct Rule Configuration was selected.
  • Confirm the correct scope was selected.
  • Confirm you modified the correct target field.
  • Review Rule History.
  • Verify that another scoped rule is not overriding the changed rule.

When necessary, close and reopen the configuration before testing again.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: A MAP rule does not return a target value.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Verify:

  • Mapping file exists
  • Mapping path is correct
  • Key column exists
  • Value column exists
  • Source value exists in the mapping
  • Source field is correct

Example:

Mapping:

A → 01
B → 02
C → 03

If the source contains:

X

there is no configured result.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: The generated migration contains fewer records than expected.

docs.title: Check FILTER Rules
docs.text:
FILTER rules determine which records continue through the migration.

Remember:

source == "20"

means:

Keep rows where source equals 20.

It does not mean:

Remove rows where source equals 20.

docs.title: Compare Record Counts
docs.text:
For example:

Source Records:       10,000
After FILTER Rules:    8,450
Generated Records:     8,450

The migration team should understand why:

1,550

records were excluded.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: The migration stops because no records remain after filtering.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Review all FILTER rules.

When multiple filters exist:

Original Data
     │
     ▼
Filter 1
     │
     ▼
Filter 2
     │
     ▼
Filter 3
     │
     ▼
0 Records

Each filter reduces the remaining population.

Test the filters individually if necessary.

docs.title: Source Does Not Appear in Standard Migration
Check
docs.text:
Verify:

config/source_map.csv

Confirm:

  • The file exists
  • MCO_SHEET exists
  • The expected business object is configured
  • The CSV was saved correctly

Then refresh the source list.

docs.title: Source Cannot Be Loaded
docs.text:
If the source appears but cannot be loaded, verify:

  • SOURCE_FILE is correct
  • File exists
  • File is accessible
  • File is not corrupted
  • File format is supported
  • SQL configuration is valid when using SQL:

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Verify:

config/migration_map.csv

Confirm the relationship between:

MCO_SHEET
API_NAME
SDT_TEMPLATE
TRANSACTION_SHEET

The selected MCO business object must resolve to the correct migration configuration.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: The migration cannot locate the required SDT workbook.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Verify that the expected template exists under:

config/sdt_templates/

Also check the SDT_TEMPLATE value in:

config/migration_map.csv

Confirm the filename matches the actual template.

docs.title: Symptom
docs.text: The SDT workbook exists, but the migration cannot populate the expected worksheet.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Verify:

TRANSACTION_SHEET

in the Migration Map.

The configured sheet name must correspond to the expected worksheet in the SDT template.

Be especially careful with:

  • Spaces
  • Spelling
  • Multiple transaction sheets

docs.title: Check Database Configuration
docs.text:
Verify:

config/db_config.ini

Check:

  • ODBC driver
  • Server
  • Database
  • Trusted Connection

Also verify that:

sqlalchemy
pyodbc

are installed.

docs.title: SQL Query Works but Rules Return Blank
docs.text:
The SQL query may not be returning all fields required by the Rule Configuration.

Example:

SELECT
    MBITNO,
    MBSTAT
FROM MITMAS

But the rule expects:

MBPUIT

MBPUIT is not available.

Review the dependencies of the affected rules and compare them with the SQL query output.

docs.title: Check
docs.text:
Verify:

  • Output directory exists
  • User has write permission
  • Existing file is not locked
  • Excel does not have the output file open
  • Sufficient disk space is available

The normal output location is:

output/

docs.title: Migration Runs but Output Is Incorrect
docs.text:
This is one of the most important troubleshooting scenarios.

A message indicating that the migration completed successfully means the application completed the processing workflow.

It does not guarantee that every business transformation is correct.

Use:

Source
   │
   ▼
Expected Business Rule
   │
   ▼
Expected Result
   │
   ↕
Actual Output

For example:

Source:

ITNO = AP32508
ITTY = FG
PUIT = 1

Requirement:

FG + PUIT 1 → PLCD 02

Expected:

PLCD = 02

Actual:

PLCD = 01

This should be treated as a rule/configuration problem even if no application error occurred.

docs.title: Use Load by ID for Troubleshooting
docs.text:
When investigating a specific record, avoid repeatedly processing the complete dataset.

Use:

Run Migration → Load by ID

to isolate representative records.

For example:

AP32508

Then review:

Raw Source
    ↓
Rule Dependencies
    ↓
Rule Logic
    ↓
Expected Value
    ↓
Actual Value

This is usually much easier than troubleshooting thousands of records at once.

docs.title: After a Rule Change
docs.text:
Whenever a rule is corrected:

Modify Rule
    │
    ▼
Save
    │
    ▼
Load by ID
    │
    ▼
Test Special Cases
    │
    ▼
Standard Migration
    │
    ▼
Validate Output

Do not immediately move from a rule change to a production migration.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Checklist
docs.text:
When a generated value is incorrect, use this checklist:

  • [ ] Am I looking at the correct raw source record?
  • [ ] Is the correct Source Map entry being used?
  • [ ] Is the correct Migration Map entry being used?
  • [ ] Is the correct Rule Configuration selected?
  • [ ] Is TARGET_FIELD correct?
  • [ ] Is SOURCE_FIELD correct?
  • [ ] Is RULE_TYPE correct?
  • [ ] Is RULE_VALUE correct?
  • [ ] Are all rule dependencies available?
  • [ ] Is the correct scope selected?
  • [ ] Are FILTER rules changing the population?
  • [ ] Is the SDT template correct?
  • [ ] Is the correct transaction sheet being populated?
  • [ ] Does the expected result match the approved business requirement?

docs.title: Recommended Troubleshooting Order
docs.text:
Avoid changing rules immediately when an output value looks wrong.

Follow this order:

1. Raw Source
      ↓
2. Source Field
      ↓
3. Rule Dependencies
      ↓
4. Business Requirement
      ↓
5. Rule Configuration
      ↓
6. Scope
      ↓
7. Expected Result
      ↓
8. Actual Output

Only modify the rule after identifying where the difference originates.

This helps prevent fixing one scenario while unintentionally breaking another.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions
docs.text:
This page provides quick answers to common questions when working with the Data Migration Tool.

For more detailed troubleshooting, see Common Errors and Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Why is my target field blank?
docs.text:
Check the Rule Configuration first.

Verify:

TARGET_FIELD
SOURCE_FIELD
RULE_TYPE
RULE_VALUE
SCOPE

Then confirm that the expected SOURCE_FIELD actually exists in the source data.

For a Python rule, also verify every field accessed through row.

Example:

puit = str(row.get("MBPUIT", "")).strip()

If MBPUIT does not exist in the source, the rule receives a blank value.

docs.title: Why is my Python rule returning the wrong value?
docs.text:
Check:

  1. Source values
  2. Source column names
  3. String versus numeric comparisons
  4. Spaces and capitalization
  5. Condition order
  6. Rule dependencies
  7. Selected scope

For example:

puit = str(row.get("MBPUIT", "")).strip()

should normally be compared with:

if puit == "3":

not:

if puit == 3:

docs.title: Why does condition order matter?
docs.text:
Python rules execute from top to bottom.

Example:

if puit == "3":
    return "05"

if itty == "FG" and puit == "3":
    return "02"

The second condition will never execute when PUIT = 3 because the first condition already returned a result.

Place higher-priority conditions before more general conditions.

docs.title: Why does the rule work for GLOBAL but not for my division?
docs.text:
A business-unit-specific rule may be overriding the GLOBAL rule.

For example:

PLCD / GLOBAL
PLCD / DIV_US

When:

Scope = DIV_US

the DIV_US rule takes precedence for PLCD.

Verify both the selected migration scope and the SCOPE value in the Rule Configuration.

docs.title: When should I use DIRECT?
docs.text:
Use DIRECT when the source value can be transferred directly to the target field without additional business logic.

Example:

MBITNO → ITNO

docs.title: When should I use CONST?
docs.text:
Use CONST when every processed record should receive the same value.

Example:

CONO = 100

docs.title: When should I use MAP?
docs.text:
Use MAP when source values need to be translated using a lookup table.

Example:

A → 01
B → 02
C → 03

MAP is generally preferable to writing a long Python rule containing many simple value-to-value conversions.

docs.title: When should I use PYTHON?
docs.text:
Use PYTHON when the target value depends on:

  • Multiple fields
  • Conditional logic
  • String manipulation
  • Special business requirements
  • More complex transformations

For example:

ITNO ──┐
ITTY ──┼──► PYTHON ──► PLCD
PUIT ──┘

docs.title: When should I use FILTER?
docs.text:
Use FILTER when certain source records should not continue through the migration.

Remember that the filter expression represents records to keep.

Example:

source == "20"

means:

Keep records where the source value is 20.

docs.title: Why are records missing from my output?
docs.text:
Check the number of records at each stage:

Source
   │
   ▼
FILTER Rules
   │
   ▼
Remaining Records
   │
   ▼
Output

FILTER rules are one of the first things to investigate when the output contains fewer records than expected.

docs.title: Why did the migration say all rows were filtered out?
docs.text:
Your FILTER rules removed every source record.

Review each filter individually and confirm that the conditions represent records that should be kept.

docs.title: Why doesn't my source appear in Standard Migration?
docs.text:
Check:

config/source_map.csv

Verify that the expected business object exists under:

MCO_SHEET

Then refresh the source list.

docs.title: What is the difference between Source Map and Migration Map?
docs.text:
The Source Map determines where the data comes from.

MCO Sheet → Legacy Source

The Migration Map determines which M3 configuration should process it.

MCO Sheet
   │
   ├── API
   ├── SDT Template
   └── Transaction Sheets

Together:

Source Map
    │
    ▼
Legacy Data
    │
    ▼
Migration Map
    │
    ▼
M3 Configuration

docs.title: Why can't the tool find my SDT template?
docs.text:
Check:

config/migration_map.csv

and verify the configured:

SDT_TEMPLATE

Then confirm that the template exists under:

config/sdt_templates/

docs.title: Why can't the tool find the transaction sheet?
docs.text:
Verify:

TRANSACTION_SHEET

in the Migration Map.

The configured worksheet must exist in the corresponding SDT template.

Check spelling and spaces carefully.

docs.title: Can I use Excel, CSV, and SQL as sources?
docs.text:
Yes. The migration source can be configured from supported file sources or SQL.

SQL sources use:

SQL:

For example:

SQL:SELECT * FROM MITMAS

SQL connectivity also requires the database configuration to be available.

docs.title: Why does my SQL migration return blank fields?
docs.text:
Confirm that the SQL query returns every source column required by the rules.

For example, if a rule needs:

MBPUIT

but the query only returns:

SELECT MBITNO, MBSTAT
FROM MITMAS

then MBPUIT is unavailable to the rule.

docs.title: How can I test one problematic record?
docs.text:
Use:

Run Migration → Load by ID

This is useful when troubleshooting records such as:

AP32508

Instead of reviewing thousands of rows, you can focus on:

Source Record
     ↓
Rule Dependencies
     ↓
Expected Result
     ↓
Actual Result

docs.title: Should I test a rule before running a complete migration?
docs.text:
Yes.

A recommended workflow is:

Modify Rule
    │
    ▼
Load by ID
    │
    ▼
Validate Test Cases
    │
    ▼
Standard Migration
    │
    ▼
Validate Output

Use representative records for each important business condition.

docs.title: When should I use Auto-Detect?
docs.text:
Use Auto-Detect when you have a legacy source file but are unsure which configured migration object should process it.

Auto-Detect analyzes source-field signatures and attempts to identify the appropriate migration context.

The detected configuration should still be verified before migration.

docs.title: When should I use Batch Migration?
docs.text:
Use Batch Migration after the individual migrations have already been configured and tested.

Recommended progression:

Develop
   ↓
Load by ID
   ↓
Standard Migration
   ↓
Validate
   ↓
Batch Migration

Batch Migration should not normally be the first test of a new Rule Configuration.

docs.title: Should I create a snapshot before changing rules?
docs.text:
For significant changes, yes.

For example:

Current Rules
     │
     ▼
Snapshot
     │
     ▼
Modify Rules
     │
     ▼
Test

Snapshots provide a reference to the previous Rule Configuration.

docs.title: What should I do after Sync / Merge?
docs.text:
Identify which rules changed and retest those fields.

Recommended process:

Merge
  ↓
Identify Changes
  ↓
Load by ID
  ↓
Validate
  ↓
Standard Migration

A successful merge does not automatically mean the resulting migration values are correct.

docs.title: Where are generated migration files saved?
docs.text:
Generated migration files are normally stored under:

output/

Check the System Log after migration to confirm the generated output location.

docs.title: Why can't the output file be saved?
docs.text:
Check whether:

  • The file is already open in Excel
  • The output folder is accessible
  • You have write permission
  • An existing output file is locked

Closing the workbook in Excel often resolves file-locking issues.

docs.title: Does "Migration Completed" mean the migration is correct?
docs.text:
No.

It means the application completed the processing workflow successfully.

You should still validate:

Record Counts
      +
Required Fields
      +
Transformation Rules
      +
Business Requirements
      +
SDT Structure
      │
      ▼
Validated Migration

Technical success and business correctness are different.

docs.title: What Should I Check Before Saying a Migration Is Ready?
docs.text:
Use this final checklist:

  • [ ] Correct source selected
  • [ ] Correct MCO business object
  • [ ] Correct API
  • [ ] Correct Rule Configuration
  • [ ] Correct scope
  • [ ] FILTER population validated
  • [ ] Important Python rules tested
  • [ ] MAP values validated
  • [ ] Record counts validated
  • [ ] Required fields populated
  • [ ] SDT template correct
  • [ ] Transaction sheets correct
  • [ ] Representative records validated
  • [ ] Output file opens successfully
  • [ ] System Log reviewed for warnings or errors

A migration should be considered ready only after both the application execution and the resulting business data have been validated.

docs.title: Need More Detail?
docs.text:
See:

  • Common Errors and Troubleshooting
  • Python Rules
  • MAP Rules
  • FILTER Rules
  • Load by ID
  • Rule History

docs.title: Copy Sheet Utility
docs.text:
The Copy Sheet utility is used to copy worksheet data between Excel workbooks as part of migration preparation or file-management activities.

This utility operates independently from the main migration process.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Migration work often requires moving data from one workbook into another while preparing source files, templates, or supporting migration files.

The Copy Sheet utility simplifies this process.

Source Workbook
      │
      ▼
Select Worksheet
      │
      ▼
Copy Sheet
      │
      ▼
Destination Workbook

docs.title: Accessing the Utility
docs.text:
Navigate to:

Utilities → Copy Sheet

The utility provides the controls required to select the source and destination Excel files.

docs.title: Typical Use Cases
docs.text:
Copy Sheet can be useful when:

  • Preparing migration workbooks
  • Moving data between Excel files
  • Consolidating migration information
  • Reusing an existing worksheet
  • Preparing supporting files for testing
  • Avoiding manual Excel copy-and-paste operations

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
The general process is:

Select Source File
       │
       ▼
Select Source Sheet
       │
       ▼
Select Destination
       │
       ▼
Copy
       │
       ▼
Review Result

docs.title: Source Workbook
docs.text:
Select the Excel workbook containing the worksheet that should be copied.

For example:

Legacy_Item_Data.xlsx

The workbook may contain several worksheets:

Legacy_Item_Data.xlsx
│
├── Item Master
├── Item Facility
└── Item Warehouse

Select the worksheet required for the operation.

docs.title: Destination Workbook
docs.text:
Select the workbook that should receive the copied worksheet.

For example:

Migration_Workbook.xlsx

The selected sheet is then copied into the destination workbook according to the utility's configured behavior.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
After copying a worksheet, verify:

  • The expected worksheet exists in the destination workbook.
  • Column headers were preserved.
  • The expected number of records was copied.
  • Important values were preserved.
  • The destination workbook remains valid.

For migration-related data, comparing row counts is recommended:

Source Sheet
12,450 rows

Destination Sheet
12,450 rows

Unexpected differences should be investigated.

docs.title: Important Consideration
docs.text:
The Copy Sheet utility performs a file-preparation operation.

It does not apply migration transformation rules.

Copy Sheet
    │
    └── Moves worksheet data

Migration Engine
    │
    └── Applies transformation rules

These are separate processes.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
When using Copy Sheet:

  1. Confirm the correct source workbook.
  2. Confirm the correct source worksheet.
  3. Confirm the destination workbook.
  4. Perform the copy.
  5. Review the resulting workbook.
  6. Validate row counts when applicable.
  7. Preserve the original source file when possible.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If the operation fails, verify:

  • The source workbook exists.
  • The destination workbook exists or is valid for the requested operation.
  • The selected worksheet exists.
  • The workbook is not locked by another application.
  • The user has permission to access the files.
  • The files are valid Excel workbooks.

If Excel has the destination workbook open, close it and retry the operation.

docs.title: Relationship to Migration
docs.text:
Copy Sheet can support migration preparation, but it is not part of the transformation pipeline.

Preparation Utilities
        │
        ▼
Prepared Source Files
        │
        ▼
Data Migration Tool
        │
        ▼
Transformation Rules
        │
        ▼
M3 SDT Output

Use this utility when workbook preparation is required before or after the main migration process.

docs.title: Merge Files Utility
docs.text:
The Merge Files utility is used to combine migration-related files into a single consolidated file.

This utility supports file preparation and consolidation activities and operates separately from the main migration transformation process.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
During migration activities, data may be distributed across multiple files that need to be combined.

Conceptually:

File 1 ──┐
File 2 ──┼──► Merge Files ──► Combined File
File 3 ──┘

The Merge Files utility provides a controlled way to perform this consolidation from within the Data Migration Tool.

docs.title: Accessing the Utility
docs.text:
Navigate to:

Utilities → Merge Files

Use the interface to select the files that should participate in the merge operation.

docs.title: Typical Use Cases
docs.text:
Merge Files can be useful when:

  • Migration data has been delivered in multiple files
  • Multiple extracts belong to the same dataset
  • Migration results need to be consolidated
  • Test files need to be combined
  • Supporting migration files need to be prepared

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
The general workflow is:

Select Files
     │
     ▼
Review Selection
     │
     ▼
Merge
     │
     ▼
Combined File
     │
     ▼
Validate Result

docs.title: Selecting Files
docs.text:
Select the files that should be included in the merge.

Before proceeding, verify that the selected files belong to the same intended dataset or migration activity.

For example:

ItemMaster_Part1.xlsx
ItemMaster_Part2.xlsx
ItemMaster_Part3.xlsx

can represent different portions of the same source dataset.

docs.title: Data Compatibility
docs.text:
Files being combined should have compatible structures.

For example:

File 1

ITNO | ITTY | PUIT

File 2

ITNO | ITTY | PUIT

These structures can logically be consolidated because the columns represent the same data.

Be careful when files contain different structures:

File 1

ITNO | ITTY | PUIT

File 2

CUNO | CUNM | STAT

These represent different datasets and should not normally be treated as one migration source.

docs.title: Validation After Merge
docs.text:
Always review the resulting file after a merge operation.

Verify:

  • Expected files were included
  • Column structure is correct
  • Records were not unintentionally omitted
  • Unexpected duplicate records were not introduced
  • The resulting file can be opened successfully

docs.title: Record Count Validation
docs.text:
Record counts provide a useful first validation.

For example:

File 1     5,000 rows
File 2     4,000 rows
File 3     3,000 rows
           ──────────
Expected  12,000 rows

The merged result should contain the expected population, accounting for any headers or other structural behavior of the merge process.

!!! important Record count validation does not guarantee that the data is correct, but unexpected differences should always be investigated.

docs.title: Duplicate Records
docs.text:
Combining multiple files can potentially introduce duplicate business records.

For example:

File 1
AP32508

File 2
AP32508

After consolidation:

AP32508
AP32508

Whether this is valid depends on the source and migration requirement.

The merge operation should therefore be followed by business-key validation when duplicate records are a concern.

docs.title: Merge Files vs Migration
docs.text:
The Merge Files utility does not replace the migration transformation process.

Merge Files
     │
     ▼
Combined Dataset
     │
     ▼
Migration Engine
     │
     ▼
Rule Configuration
     │
     ▼
M3 Output

The merge prepares or consolidates data.

The Migration Engine applies transformation rules.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
Before merging:

  1. Confirm all files belong to the intended dataset.
  2. Review their column structures.
  3. Record the source row counts.
  4. Perform the merge.
  5. Review the resulting structure.
  6. Validate the resulting row count.
  7. Check important business keys for unexpected duplicates.
  8. Preserve the original files.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If a merge operation fails, verify:

  • All selected files exist
  • The files are accessible
  • The files use supported formats
  • Files are not locked by another application
  • The user has permission to read and write the required locations

If the merge completes but the result is unexpected, compare:

Individual Source Files
          │
          ▼
Expected Structure / Count
          │
          ▼
Merged Result

This helps identify which input file introduced the difference.

docs.title: Important Consideration
docs.text:
The exact merge behavior depends on the implementation of the utility.

Before relying on the result for production migration, verify how the utility handles:

  • Column differences
  • Worksheet selection
  • Headers
  • Duplicate records
  • Blank rows

The resulting file should always be validated before it becomes a migration source.

docs.title: Next Step
docs.text: Continue to Script Library to learn about the reusable migration utilities and scripts available within the Data Migration Tool.

docs.title: Script Library
docs.text:
The Script Library provides access to reusable scripts and utilities that support data migration activities.

These scripts are intended for tasks that do not necessarily belong to the standard migration workflow but are useful during data preparation, analysis, validation, or troubleshooting.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Not every migration task requires a complete migration process.

Sometimes a specific operation is needed:

Migration Task
      │
      ▼
Reusable Script
      │
      ▼
Processed Result

The Script Library provides a central location for these supporting tools.

docs.title: Accessing the Script Library
docs.text:
Navigate to:

Utilities → Script Library

The available scripts can then be reviewed and executed according to their intended purpose.

docs.title: Why Use a Script Library?
docs.text:
During migration development, small utilities are often created to solve specific problems.

Without a central library, these scripts can become scattered across:

Personal folders
Downloads
Temporary directories
Test folders
Desktop

A Script Library provides a more controlled approach:

Data Migration Tool
        │
        ▼
   Script Library
        │
        ├── Script A
        ├── Script B
        ├── Script C
        └── Script D

This makes useful migration utilities easier to find and reuse.

docs.title: Typical Script Uses
docs.text:
Scripts may support activities such as:

  • Data preparation
  • File manipulation
  • Data validation
  • Migration analysis
  • Data comparison
  • Troubleshooting
  • Repetitive migration tasks

The exact functionality depends on the scripts currently available in the library.

docs.title: Script Library vs Migration Rules
docs.text: Scripts and migration rules serve different purposes.

docs.title: Migration Rules
docs.text:
Migration rules determine how source records are transformed into M3 values.

For example:

MBPUIT
   │
   ▼
PYTHON Rule
   │
   ▼
PLCD

Rules belong to the migration transformation process.

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text:
Scripts perform supporting operations outside the normal field-level transformation process.

Source / Migration File
          │
          ▼
        Script
          │
          ▼
Processed / Analyzed Result

A reusable script should not replace a Rule Configuration when the logic belongs to the normal migration transformation.

docs.title: Before Running a Script
docs.text:
Before executing a script, understand:

  1. What the script does.
  2. What input it requires.
  3. What output it produces.
  4. Whether it modifies an existing file.
  5. Whether the operation can be reversed.
  6. Whether the result needs additional validation.

!!! warning Do not run an unfamiliar script against production migration files without first understanding its purpose and expected result.

docs.title: Input Files
docs.text:
Some scripts may require an input file.

For example:

Input File
    │
    ▼
Script
    │
    ▼
Output File

Always verify that the selected input corresponds to the purpose of the script.

Preserving the original file before running a modification script is recommended.

docs.title: Output Validation
docs.text:
The output of a script should be validated before being used in a migration.

For example:

Original Data
      │
      ▼
Run Script
      │
      ▼
Generated Result
      │
      ▼
Validate
      │
      ▼
Use in Migration

Validation may include:

  • Row counts
  • Column names
  • Business keys
  • Expected values
  • File structure
  • Duplicate records

docs.title: Script Documentation
docs.text:
Each reusable script should ideally document:

Information Description Name Script name Purpose What problem it solves Input Required file or data Output What the script generates Changes Data Whether source data is modified Usage How to run it Validation What should be checked afterward

For example:

Script: Example Utility

Purpose:
Prepare source data for migration.

Input:
Legacy Excel file.

Output:
Processed Excel file.

Validation:
Compare source and output record counts.

docs.title: Adding New Scripts
docs.text:
When a reusable migration utility is created, consider adding it to the Script Library instead of keeping it as an isolated personal script.

Before adding a script:

  1. Confirm that the operation is reusable.
  2. Give the script a descriptive name.
  3. Define its expected input.
  4. Define its expected output.
  5. Add appropriate error handling.
  6. Test the script.
  7. Document its purpose.
  8. Define how its result should be validated.

docs.title: Recommended Practice
docs.text:
Use the Script Library for supporting migration utilities.

Use the Rule Configuration for data transformation logic that belongs to the migration itself.

A useful distinction is:

Does this determine an M3 target value?
              │
       ┌──────┴──────┐
       │             │
      Yes            No
       │             │
       ▼             ▼
Migration Rule    Utility Script

This helps keep migration logic centralized and maintainable.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If a script fails:

  • Verify the correct script was selected.
  • Verify the required input was provided.
  • Check that input files exist.
  • Check that files are not locked.
  • Verify read/write permissions.
  • Review any error message produced by the script.

If the script completes but the result is unexpected, do not immediately use the output for migration.

Compare:

Expected Result
       ↕
Actual Result

and investigate the difference first.

docs.title: Utilities Summary
docs.text:
The Utilities section provides supporting functionality around the core migration process:

Utilities
│
├── Copy Sheet
│
├── Merge Files
│
└── Script Library

These tools assist with preparing and managing migration data but remain separate from the core Rule Configuration and transformation process.
